REPORT OF THE PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE ON THE REPORT OF THE AUDITOR-GENERAL ON THE STATEMENT OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RECEIPTS AND PAYMENTS OF THE BANK OF GHAN FOR THE YEAR ENDED 
315" DECEMBER 2024 

INTRODUCTION 

The Report of the Auditor-General on the Consolidated Statements of Foreign Exchange 
Receipts and Payments of the Bank of Ghana for the year ended 315 December, 2024 was 
presented to Parliament on Thursday, 3" July, 2025 in accordance with article 184(3) of the 1992 Constitution by the Hon Majority Leader and MP for Bawku Central, Mr Mahama 
Ayariga. H 

Pursuant to Order 229 of the Standing Orders of Parliament, the Report of the Auditor-General 
was referred to the Public Accounts Committee for consideration and report. 

DELIBERATIONS 

The Committee expresses its gratitude to the Deputy Minister for Finance, Mr Thomas Nyarko 
Ampem, officials from tHe Ministry of Finance, Bank of Ghana and Ghana Revenue Authority 
for attending the Hearing and assisting the Committee. 

REFERENCE DOCUMENTS 
The Committee referred to the following documents during its deliberations: 
i. The Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992; 
ii.  The Standing Orders of the Parliament of Ghana, 2024; 
iii.  The Bank of Ghana Act, 2002 (Act 612) as amended by the Bank of Ghana 

(Amendment) Act, 2025 (Act 1158); 
iv. The Audit Service Act, 2000 (Act 584); 
V. The Foreign Exchange Act, 2006 (Act 723); 
vi.  The Minerals and Mining Law, 1986 (PNDC Law 153); and 
vii.  The Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703). 

BACKGROUND 

The audit was planned and performed to obtain reasonable assurance that the Statements of 
Foreign Exchange Recelpts and Payments, taken as a whole, were free fiom material 
misstatements, The desigh and maintenance of internal control system to safeguard foreign 
exchange resources and the preparation of accurate and reliable records are the responsibility 
of the Directors of the Bank of Ghana, 

The Statements of Foreignt Exchange Receipts and Payments of the Bank of Ghana (BoG) for 
the year ended 31 December 2024 were audited in compliance with Article 184 (3) of the 1992 
Constitution of the Repub‘ic of Ghana and Section 12(2) of the Audit Service Act, 2000 (Act 
584). The audit is for a full year encompassing gross Foreign Exchange Receipts and Payments 
of the Bank of Ghana front 1 January to 31 December 2024.

PURPOSE OF THE AUDIT 

The audit was to ascertain the effectiveness of the control systems put in place by the Bank of 

Ghana per its mandate, to safeguard our foreign exchange and whether the records in that 

respect, is accurate and fairly represents the financial situation of our forex. 

SCOPE OF AUDIT 

The audit covered the period 1* January, 2024 to 31 December, 2024 and it was on the receipts 

and payments of foreign exchange by the Bank of Ghana. 

OVERVIEW OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RECEIPTS AND PAYMENTS 

Foreign Exchange Receipts 

In the year under review, the Bank of Ghana’s foreign exchange inflows were derived from 

Export Receipts through Bank of Ghana (cocoa and minerals), GoG Loan Inflows, BoG Short 

Term Financing Facilities and Dividends and Forex Purchases and Earnings on 

Correspondence Accounts. 

The total inflows for 2024 was US$11,996,058,801.11 as compared to US$8,411,303,953.54 

for 2023 and it demonstrated an improvement in forex receipts. A breakdown of the total 

inflows for 2024 indicates that Forex Purchases and Earnings on Correspondence Accounts of 

US$4,986.63 million contributed 41.57% as compared to US$3,205.83 million or 38.11% 

recorded in 2023. The decrease was as a result of the reclassification and introduction of 

additional line-items, which moved gold and oil-related inflows from forex purchases to 

Minerals.

Export Receipts and Payments 

The Committee observed that quantum of Export receipts surrendered to the BoG for Cocoa 

and Minerals for 2024 was US$6.1 billion. On the quantum surrendered for 2025, the Governor 

of the Bank of Ghana informed the Committee that the figures are yet to be audited. On whether 

the quantum surrendered for 2025 was expected to be higher than that of 2024, the Governor 

reiterated that he will revert when the audit is completed. He requested to be afforded the 

opportunity to meet with the Committee again after the audit in order to provide the 

information. 

On whether the oil revenues for 2025 exceeded the amount of US$495,602,219.72 for 2024, 

the Governor says it basically has to with prices and volumes. He requested again to be afforded 

the opportunity to meet with the Committee again and provided further details on the matter 

and other such ones. 

The Committee observed that as shown on Table 1 Foreign Exchange receipts for 2024 was 

USS$ 11.9 billion relative to the amount of US$8.4 billion recorded in 2023 and therefore an 

increase of about US$3.6 billion over the period which translates into 42.6%. The Governor 

informed the Committee that, the external sector position improved in 2025. He said our 

commodity prices have fared well throughout 2025 and consistent details have already been 

provided in the press releases of the Monetary Policy Committee. 

Payments for Services and Works 

The Committee observed that the Bank’s payment projection for Services and Works for the 

year 2024 was US$1,267,230,000.00, whilst the actual payment amounted to 

US$1,771,961,226.31, showing a difference of US$504,731,226.31 which translates into 

39.83%. The Committee was informed that the payments are made up of manpower training 

and development, embassy transfers, progress payments to contractors, management and 

technical service fees, institutional subscriptions and sundry payments, 

Total payments for Services and Works for the year 2024 were US$1,771,961,226.31 

compared with US$1,192,534,511.54 recorded in 2023, indicating an increase of 

US$579,426,714.77 or 48.59%. The increase resulted from a rise jn non- surrendered and 

sundry payments. 

On the issue of payments for projects, the Governor said the Central Bank must verify 

completion and collect the necessary documentation before making payment as instructed by 

the Controller and Accountant-General. He explained further that the Central Bank is to ensure 

that the underlying vouchers are what they are supposed to be and also the instructions follow 

what controller has authorised. The Governor informed the Committee that the Central Bank 

has a risk management department that also screens payments. He said the Bank strictly goes 

by the documentation and added that the issue of cost and value for money for the project does 

not come in at all when it comes to the responsibility of the Bank.

The Committee inquired dbout the payment of an amount of US$49,199,790.12 in year 2024 
in respect of Managenent and Technical Services as compared to the amount of 
US$41,583,961.96 incurréd in 2023 for services of such like and the reason for the increase of 
US$7,615,828.16 which ttanslates into 18.31% over the period. The Officials of the Bank of 
Ghana explained that they include remuneration of consultants and payments for the provision 
of services of a technical hature, for example payments for some softwatres, including Reuters 
and Bloomberg. They inkormed the Committee that the payments are also in respect of the 
technical assistance on the Presidential Air Force Plane as well as other engagements. He made 
a request to be afforded dnother opportunity to appear before the Committee and make other 
details available. 

Unearned Salaries and Recoveries Made into the Auditor-General’s Recovery Account 

at the Bank of Ghana 

The Committee raised issues related to salaries paid to people who have not earned them or to 
people who have vacated their post or left government employment, also classified as unearned 
salaries or salaries paid in error. The issues include challenges including delays associated with 
paying back those moniés by the commercial banks into government coffers. Since the Bank 
of Ghana is the Regulator of commercial banks in the Country, the Committee requested for 
its support to ensure that such monies are paid back into the Auditor-General’s Recovery 
Account at the Central Bank without problems or challenges, when proof is shown to the 
commercial banks, 

Export Promotion by the Commercial Banks 

On efforts being made by the Bank of Ghana to promote exports, the Governor informed the 
Committee that the Certral Bank has already met with the commercial banks and taken 
submissions from them to that effect. He said the Central Bank is effectively monitoring the 
activities indicated in their submissions geared towards export promotion. He assured the 
Committee his team is working assiduously to ensure that the commercial banks are not just 
doing banking but operate to help achieve the objectives of the Bank of Ghana. He cited an 
example that we should Have a situation where a commercial bank in Ghana with South Africa 
origin would be able to assist Ghanaian firms that wants to go into the South African market 
because it understands the South African market better. He also said the Central Bank will 
continue to work with the commercial banks to ensure effective collaboration to achieve 
desired results. 

IMF Structural Benchnarks or Performance Criteria and the Responsibility of the Bank 
of Ghana 

The Committee inquired from the Bank of Ghana, progress made with respect to the IMF's 
structural benchmarks slnce January 2025 and where implementation risks remain. The 
Governor responded that some aspects of the structural benchmarks relate to the mandate of 
the Bank of Ghana and others relate to the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) and other 
agencies. He said he coultl only confirm to the Committee the Central Bank is up to date with

10.7 

10.8 

109 

the structural benchmarks that concerns its operations. He indicated that at the end of the most 

recent review, no queries were raised by the Team from IMF. 

Gold for Qil and Gold for Reserves 

The Governor provided details to the Committee on the net losses for the gold for oil and the 

gold for reserves. He informed the Committee that in 2022, the net loss for the gold for oil was 

about GHC74.44 million. There was no net loss for the gold for reserves in the period. He said 

in 2023, the net loss for the gold for oil was GH(317.69 million, whilst the net loss for the 

gold for reserves was about GHC1.54 billion. 

He indicated that in 2024, the net loss for the gold for oil was GH(1.8 billion, whilst the net 

loss for the gold for reserves in the same period was GHC3.8 billion. He reiterated that the data 

for 2025 was under audit and for that matter the Bank of Ghana had to wait until the audit is 

over. He indicated that the Central Bank would publish its financials by March 2026 and the 

Committee would have the opportunity to purse the details. 

The Governor admitted that operations such as the gold for oil programme, substitute direct 

fiscal financing and are quasi-fiscal activities or interventions introduced to address some 

specific issues. He said the losses are not new and that they existed before 2025. He opined the 

issue was not about the losses but how the schemes would be reformed to become more 

efficient going forward. He stated that it is high time we do some review to further reduce the 

cost involved, if possible and devise some other strategies to make it more impactful. He said 

the Bank of Ghana have had to bring certain aspects of the programme to an end and added 

that a number of options are being considered as part of efforts aimed at reforming the schemes 

for more benefits in terms of economic stabilization and reserve build-up. He explained that 

even though in 2024, the net loss for the gold for oil was GHC1.8 billion and that of the gold 

for reserves was GH('3.8 billion in the same period and therefore costlier, the gold for reserves 

was not terminated because the latter is aimed at building reserves. 

He said the Central Bank since the beginning of 2026, has been devising ways of reducing its 

charges and sustaining them at appreciable levels to benefit Ghanaians and that is evidenced 

by the decline in the lending rate. 

Gold Smuggling 

The Governor informed the Committee that, the Central Bank is making efforts to close all 

gaps exploited by gold smugglers to avoid the losses we make as a result of the canker. He 

indicated that what we have lost as a Country by way of leakages over the years, is mind- 

blowing. 

The Reserve and Asset Position of the Bank of Ghana 

On the BOG's reserve asset position achieved with the various interventions that have come 

into play in the course of the year 2024, the Governor referred to the Auditor-General’s Report 

on the Bank which says the asset position is US$8.6 billion. The reserve position of the Bank 

as at the end of December 2025, stood at US$13.829 billion. 

Page 6 of 8

11.0  CONCLUSION 

For a Statement on Foreigh Exchange Receipts and Payments of BOG to be used as a reliable 
source of information fof decision-making by policy makers and other stakeholders, the 
Committee is of the opihion that it should be devoid of errors, omissions and wrongful 
treatment of transactions. 

The Committee therefore urges the Bank of Ghana to strengthen its internal and supervisory 
control systems to avert the recurrence of errors, omissions and wrongful treatment of 
transactions in its Statements. 

The Committee thereford recommends to the House to adopt this Report on the Report of the 
Auditor-General on the Consolidated Statements of Foreign Exchange Receipts and Payments 
of the Bank of Ghana for the year ended 31% December, 2024.

INTRODUCTION 

The Performance Audit Report of the Auditor-General on the Provision and Maintenance 
of Toilet Facilities ih Public Schools was presented to the House by the Hon Majority 
Leader, Mr Mahama Ayariga, on Tuesday, 15! July, 2025 pursuant to article 187(5) of the 
1992 Constitution. 

In accordance with Order 229 of the Standing Orders of the House, the Performance 
Audit Report was subsequently referred to the Public Accounts Committee for 
examination and report. 

DELIBERATIONS 

The Committee held a public hearing to examine the referral. In appearance were the 
Hon Deputy Minister for Education, Dr Clement Apaak and Officials of the Ministry of 
Education; and Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs. 

Pursuant to Order 229(4) of the Standing Orders, the Hon Ranking Member, Mr Samuel 
Atta Mills chaired the consideration of the Special Audit Report for the period ending 
2024 which relates to the period of administration of the Chairperson of the Committee. 

The Committee expressed profound gratitude to the Hon Deputy Minister for Education; 
the Hon Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs; and the 
Officials for their attendance and assisting in the deliberations. 

REFERENCE DOCUMENTS 

The Commitee referred to the following documents during its deliberations: 

1 The Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992; 

il.  The Standing Orders of the Republic of Ghana, 2024; 
ifi.  The Audit Setvice Act, 2000 (Act 584); 

iv.  The Internal Audit Agency Act, 2003 (Act 658); 
V. The Public Procurement Act 2003 (Act 663) as amended by Act 914; 
vi.  The Value Added Tax Act, 2025 (Act 1151); and 
vii.  The Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921); 
viii. The pre-Tertiary Education Act, 202 (Act 1049); 
ix.  The Ghana Education Service Act, 1995 (Act 506); 
x.  The Children's Act, 1998 (Act 560);

xii.  Public Financial Management Regulations, 2019 (L.1. 1804); and 
xiii. The Educatioh Strategic Plan (2010-2020).

4.0  BACKGROUND INFORMATION 

5.0 

6.0 

7.0 

7.1 

The United Nations General Assembly in 2010 recognised access to safe and clean 

drinking water and sanitation as a fundamental human right essential to the full 

enjoyment of life. Given that children spend a significant portion of their day in school, 

the provision of adequate water and sanitation facilities is critical to safeguarding their 

health and creating a conducive environment for teaching and learning. 

In Ghana, the provision and management of sanitation infrastructure in schools is a 

shared responsibility among the Ministry of Sanitation and Water Resources, the 

Ministry of Education, and the Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies 

(MMDAs). The Ghana Education Service plays a key role in implementing policies and 

guidelines aimed at ensuring safe and hygienic conditions in schools across the country. 

Over the years, the Government of Ghana has established a legal and policy framework 

to address sanitation and education challenges, including the Education Service Act, 

1995 (Act 506), the Children’s Act, 1998 (Act 560), and the Education Act, 2008 (Act 

778). The introduction of the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene programme under the 

Education Strategic Plan (2010-2020), supported by development partners such as 

UNICEF and the World Bank, further demonstrates efforts to improve sanitation and 

hygiene in schools. 

Despite these interventions, challenges persist. Data from the Ghana Statistical Service 

indicate that only two out of five schools have access to adequate sanitation and water 

facilities, undermining progress towards Sustainable Development Goals Goal 6. In 

response, the Auditor-General commissioned an audit to evaluate the provision and 

maintenance of toilet facilities in public schools and to recommend measures for 

improvement. 

PURPOSE OF AUDIT 

The purpose of the audit was to ascertain whether the measures put in place by the 

Ministry of Education and Ghana Education Service (GES) have ensured that sanitary 

facilities are provided and are well maintained in public schools and make 

recommendations for improvements. 

SCOPE OF THE AUDIT 

The audit covered the Environmental Health and Sanitation Department (EHSD) of the 

Ministry of Sanitation and Water Resources (MSWR), the School Health Education 

Programme (SHEP) Unit of GES and selected schools within Metropolitan Assemblies 

of Accra, Kumasi and Tamale that are responsible for the management of sanitary 

facilities in the schools. The audit covers the period from 2019 to 2023. 

AUDIT FINDINGS AND MANAGEMENT RESPONSES 

Provision of toilet facilities 

2|Page

8.0 

8.1 

The audit identified challenges in the arcas of provision and maintenance of toilet 
facilities. On provision of toilet facilities, the Auditors found the following: 

i. Inadequate toilet facilities in schools; 

ii.  Toilets not included in school infrastructure design; 

iii. ~ Abandonment of toilet facilities due to lack of water; and 

iv.  Delay in handihg over completed toilet projects. 

On maintenance of toilet facilities, the Auditors made the following findings: 

i. Poor cleaning of toilet facilities; 

ii.  Failure to promptly repair broken or faulty fixtures; and 

iii.  Ineffective monitoring of toilet facilities. 

PROVISION OF SANITARY FACILITIES 

Inadequate sanitaty facilities in public schools 

Section 36(1) of the Pre-Tertiary Education Act, 2020 (Act 1049) mandates the provision, 
maintenance, and equipping of public schools, while the WASH in Schools Technical 
Guide (2014) presctibes a maximum ratio of one toilet to fifty pupils. The audit found 

that although the Ministry of Education, through its implementation structures, is 

responsible for school infrastructure, most public schools lack adequate sanitary 
facilities. 

Evidence from the Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly’s 2022 Annual Action Plan revealed 
a severe infrastructdre gap, with an overall toilet deficit of 94.5 percent across schools. 

Kindergarten and ptimary schools recorded the highest deficits, indicating widespread 

non-compliance with minimum sanitation standards. The following table shows the 
details:

Further analysis of 63 sampled schools showed that only 13 percent met the required 

standard, while 25 percent had no toilet facilities at all. In extreme cases, over 2,000 

students depended on a single facility. The deficits were attributed to the failure to 

3|Pag &

8.2 

include sanitation in school infrastructure projects, non-functional water closet systems 

due to lack of water, and delays in handing over completed donor-funded facilities. 

Management Response 

Management acknowledges the finding of the Auditor-general regarding inadequacy of 

toilet facilities in public schools. The ministry recognises that the provision of safe, 

adequate and accessible sanitation facilities is essential to improving teaching and 

learning outcomes. 

Management notes that the sanitation deficits identified are largely attributable to 

inadequate budgetary allocations, competing infrastructural priorities and delays in the 

release of funds for school infrastructure projects. 

Responses given by Management at the public hearing 

Management acknowledged that inadequate toilet facilities remained a significant 

challenge in some public schools across the country. They recognised that access to 

adequate sanitation is a fundamental requirement under the Pre-tertiary Education Act, 

2020 (Act 1049) as well as the WASH in Schools Technical Guidelines. 

Management however stated that the sanitation deficits highlighted by the audit is largely 

due to years of accumulated infrastructure gaps, increasing school enrolment, inadequate 

funding and competing national priorities. 

Management has intensified efforts to address these challenges. The Ministry has 

directed GES and Education Directorates in MMDAS to undertake periodic assessments 

of sanitation facilities to identify critical gaps and prioritise schools requiring urgent 

attention, 

Committee Recommendation 

The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Education and GES, in collaboration 

with MMDAs should develop and implement a time-bound action plan to eliminate the 

sanitation deficit in public schools with priority given to schools with no toilet facilities. 

Toilets not included in school infrastructure design 

The audit found that the Ministry of Education and GES failed to ensure that toilet 

facilities were included in the construction of new classroom blocks, contrary to section 

36(1) of the Pre-Tertiary Education Act, 2020 (Act 1049). Although GES is mandated to 

build, equip and maintain schools, several classroom projects executed by the Ghana 

Education Trust Fund (GETFund) and MMDAs did not include toilets. Review of plans, 

4|Page

8.3 

budgets and project reports, particularly in Kumasi and Tamale, confirmed that 

classroom infrastructure was delivered without corresponding sanitary facilities. 

Inspections further tevealed that a number of classroom blocks across the Northern, 

Greater Accra and Ashanti Regions were completed and handed over for use without 

toilets. In some instances, Management could not explain the omission, while others 

attributed it to the absence of a standard national requirement or design mandating the 

inclusion of toilet fatilities in school projects. Regional education officers also indicated 

that they often lacked access to project designs by MMDAs and were therefore unable to 

influence the inclusion of sanitation facilities. 

Management Response 

Management explalhed that, in some cases, new classroom blocks were added to existing 

schools presumed to already have toilets, while in other instances, priority was given to 

addressing urgent classroom shortages due to limited funding. As a result, toilet facilities 

were not factored into project costs. The audit concluded that this approach has 

significantly contributed to the persistent inadequacy of sanitation facilities in schools, 

as infrastructure expansion has not been matched with corresponding investment in 

essential sanitary services. 

Responses given by Management at the public hearing 

Management revealed that not all school infrastructure projects are directly designed, 

procured and supervised by GES. A significant number of school projects are 

implemented by GETFund, MMDAs and other governmental agencies. Despite this, 

Management accepted that strong coordination and oversight should have been exercised 

to ensure that all educational infrastructure projects meet the required standards before 

completion and hadding over. 

Committee Recomnendation 

The Committee recommends that all new infrastructure projects should mandatorily 

include adequate tollet facilities and reliable water supply in accordance with the WASH 

in the Schools Technical Guidelines. 

Abandonment of toilet facilities due to lack of water 

The audit revealed, that a significant number of water closet (WC) toilet facilities in 

schools were abandoned and locked up, thereby reducing access to available sanitation 

infrastructure. Inspections showed that several WC facilities across schools, including 

those in Tamale, Mamprobi and Kumasi, were not in use despite being functional. This 

situation contributed to the overall shortage of toilet facilities, as existing infrastructure 

was rendered inaccessible to pupils and students. 

The primary reason for the abandonment of these facilities was the lack of reliable water 

supply. Interviews With school authorities and SHEP coordinators indicated that when 

i 5|Page

the toilets were used without adequate water, they quickly became unhygienic and 

created discomfort within the school environment. Consequently, school authorities 

opted to lock them up. Data from the audit further showed that a significant proportion 

of schools either had no water at all or experienced irregular supply due to factors such 

as dry boreholes, inconsistent flow from taps, disconnection over unpaid bills, and 

inadequate storage systems. 

As aresult of these water challenges, students in affected schools reported that WC toilets 

were often left unflushed and unusable, forcing authorities to close them. This compelled 

students to rely on alternative facilities such as KVIPs or resort to open defecation around 

school premises. The audit therefore highlights that the absence of sustainable water 

supply systems undermines the functionality of existing sanitation infrastructure and 

worsens the sanitation situation in public schools. 

Management Response 

Management acknowledges the audit finding that some water closet (WC) toilet facilities 
in public schools were abandoned or locked due to unreliable water supply. Management 
explains that the operation of WC facilities is dependent on a regular and sustainable 
water supply, which was unavailable in some schools because of dry boreholes, 

intermittent piped water supply, disconnection of water services arising from unpaid 

bills, and inadequate water storage facilities. 

Management further notes that school authorities temporarily closed some toilet facilities 

to prevent unhygienic conditions and safeguard the health of pupils and staff. The 
Ministry, through GES, is collaborating with the Ministry of Works, Housing and Water 

Resources, MMDAs, Ghana Water Limited and other stakeholders to improve water 
supply to affected schools. Management has also directed Regional and District 
Education Directorates to ensure that the provision of sustainable water sources, 

including boreholes and storage tanks, is considered as an integral component of school 
sanitation infrastructure. Additionally, schools have been advised to prioritise the 
payment of utility bills and adopt proper maintenance plans to ensure that toilet facilities 

remain functional. 

Management Responses given at the public hearing 

Management informed the Committee that the challenge was not the failure of the toilet 
facilities themselves but the absence of reliable water supply required for the effective 

operation of WC systems. Management explained that, in many instances, school 

authorities had no option but to temporarily lock the facilities because their continued 
use without water posed serious public health risks. 

Management further stated that the Government has intensified efforts to improve water 

availability in schools through the drilling and rehabilitation of boreholes, expansion of 
piped water connections and the installation of water storage facilities in selected schools. 
The Ministry also indicated that new school infrastructure projects are being designed to 
integrate both sanitation and sustainable water supply systems. 

6Page 

8.4 

Committee Recommendation 

The Committee recothmends that, the Ministry of Education, in collaboration with GES, 
the Ministry of Wotks, Housing and Water Resources, Ghana Water Limited and the 
Metropolitan, Munic|pa[ and District Assemblies, should ensure that every school with 
WC toilet facilities has access to a reliable and sustainable water supply. It is also 
recommended that GES should establish a preventive maintenance and monitoring 
system to ensure that toilet facilities remain functional and are not abandoned due to 
avoidable water supply challenges. 

Delay in handing dver completed toilet projects 

The audit identified delays in handing over completed donor-funded toilet facilities as a 
key factor contributing to sanitation deficits in schools. While projects under the Greater 
Accra Metropolitart Area Sanitation and Water Project (GAMA-SWP) were completed 
and handed over for use, those under the Greater Accra Sustainable Sanitation and 
Livelihood Project (GASSLIP) experienced significant delays. In several schools, 
completed toilet facilitics remained unused months after completion, thereby denying 
pupils access to much-needed sanitation infrastructure. 

Specific cases highlighted included Presbyterian Boys School (Legon), Mamprobi 
Sempe Cluster of Schools, and Tema Methodist Day SHS, where completed facilities 
had not been handet! over between ten to eleven months after completion. These delays 
worsened already poor toilet-to-student ratios, forcing students to queue for limited 
facilities or resort to using public toilets outside school premises. In some cases, the 
situation contributed to open defecation and even absenteeism, as pupils left school 
premises and failed to return, 

In response, the Ministry of Education explained that the delays were partly due to 
procedural requirements, including final inspections and correction of defects before 
official handover. The Ministry assured that measures would be taken to ensure future 
projects include saftitation facilities at the planning stage and that existing deficits are 
addressed. The mihistry further indicated that the affected facilities have since been 
handed over and emphasized its commitment to improving coordination with relevant 
stakeholders to prevent recurrence, 

Management Response 

The Management fesponded that the planning and implementation of infrastructure 
projects for schools by the Ministry, ensured the inclusion of wash facilities. However, 
the projects identifled in the audit report could be mainly attributed to the. nature of 
requests received from the beneficiary MMDAS or schools. 

To prevent the recutrence of such anomalies, Management of MoE will ensure requests 
for classroom blocks include sanitary facilities. The Ministry also agreed to liaise with 
GES to ensure that sanitary facilities’ deficits in the existing schools are addressed. It 
said it will also explore sustainable measures to ensure abandoned toilet facilities are put 
to use. 

7|Page

The toilet facilities at the Presbyterian Boys® Senior High School, Legon and the 

Mamprobi Sempe Cluster of Schools in question have been handed over to the various 

beneficiary schools. The Ministry explained that when the construction of the toilet 

facilities was done, the project liaises with the Metropolitan or the Municipal Assembly 

for their handing over. A completion inspection is done on each of the facilities using a 

Snag List with the Assembly and contractors before the handing over of the facilities to 

the schools. Hence the school toilets may look complete but are not fully done until the 

contractor completes the remediation of all defaults before handing over to the schools. 

Response given to the Committee at the public hearing 

Management informed the Committee that as of August 2024, the uncompleted projects 

with toilet facilities have been completed and handed over to the schools mentioned in 

the Auditor-General’s Report considered. 

On the abandoned sanitary facility projects, the Hon Deputy Minister for Education 

informed the Committee that an audit will be carried out and appraisal will be done to 

ascertain how much it will cost the Ministry to put the structures to use. He assured the 

Ministry will work assiduously to put the sanitary facilities to use and added that 

mechanised boreholes will be constructed to provide reliable water supply at the various 

locations. 

Committee Recommendation 

The Committee observed that MoE and GES failed to ensure the provision of adequate 

toilet facilities in public schools to meet the needs of the student population, thereby 

undermining hygiene and a conducive learning environment. 

The Committee observed that toilet facilities were not consistently incorporated into the 

planning and budgeting of school infrastructure projects, resulting in classroom blocks 

being constructed without corresponding sanitation facilities. 

The Committee recommends that the FPMU of the MoE and the GES ensures that: 

i.  provision for toilet facilities is included during the planning and budgeting stages 

for school infrastructure projects; 

ii.  the MoE, GES and MMDAs collaborates to find sustainable solutions to the water 

. challenges in schools, especially in the Northern Region to facilitate the use and 

maintenance of their WC toilets; and 

iii.  they follow up on completed sanitary projects which had not been handed to the 

schools. 

8|Page

9.0 MAINTENANCE OF SANITARY FACILITIES 

i1 Poor cleaning of totlet facilities 

The audit revealed that sanitary facilities in public schools were not cleaned daily as 

required by the WASH in Schools Facilities Planning and Management Guide (2014). 

Inspections showed widespread unhygienic conditions, including faccal matter around 

toilets, unclean urinals, and littered sanitary waste. Although cleaning responsibilities 

were assigned to pupils or janitors, most schools lacked structured cleaning schedules 

and effective supervision, resulting in irregular and poorly managed sanitation practices. 

The situation was worsened by systemic and social challenges. In many schools, cleaning 

was treated as punishment for indiscipline rather than a structured responsibility, leading 

to poor supervision and ineffective outcomes. In some communities, public intrusion into 

school toilet facilities made maintenance difficult, as non-students used and sometimes 

damaged the facilities. Additionally, basic schools faced financial constraints due to 

delays in the release of capitation grants and the abolition of PTA levies, making it 

difficult to procure cleaning materials and maintain hygiene standards. 

At the senior high school level, although cleaning materials were available, poor usage 

habits and overcrowding placed excessive pressure on limited facilities, contributing to 

their unsanitary state. The audit further revealed that these conditions had serious health 

implications, with cases of infections such as diarrhoea, typhoid, and urinary tract 

infections reported among students. Overall, the findings highlight that weak supervision, 

inadequate funding, poor user behaviour, and infrastructure deficits collectively 

undermine the proper maintenance of sanitation facilities in schools. 

Management response 

Management acknowledged the findings of the Auditor-General regarding the poor 

cleaning and maintenance of toilet facilities in public schools. It noted that the challenges 

identified are largely attributable to inadequate funding, irregular release of capitation 

grants, overcrowding in schools, weak supervision, and the absence of structured 
maintenance plans in some schools. 

To address these challenges, Management has directed all Regional and District 

Education Directorates to ensure that every school develops and implements a structured 
cleaning and maintenance schedule with clearly assigned responsibilities and regular 
supervision by headteachers. 

Responses given by Management at the public hearing 

During the public ‘hearing, Management informed the Committee that the Ministry of 
Education and the Ghana Education Service have issued guidelines requiring schools to 
maintain hygienic sanitation facilities. However, compliance has been affected by 
inadequate financidl resources, delays in the release of capitation grants, increasing 

student enrolment, and the abolition of PTA levies, which previously supported the 
purchase of cleaning materials. 

9]P; 

9.2 

Management further explained that headteachers have been instructed (o establish 

sanitation committees, enforce regular cleaning schedules, and ensure closer supervision 

of pupils and janitorial staff. It also stated that environmental health officers and SHEP 

coordinators have been tasked to undertake periodic inspections and provide sanitation 

education to schools. 

Committee Recommendation 

The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Education and GES enforce mandatory 
daily cleaning and maintenance schedules in all public schools, with headteachers held 
accountable for compliance through regular monitoring by District and Regional 

Education Directorates. 

The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Finance ensure the timely 
release of capitation grants and that adequate budgetary allocations be made specifically 

for sanitation and hygiene maintenance in schools. The Ministry of Education should 

also collaborate with MMDAS to provide environmental health support, rehabilitate 

deteriorated toilet facilities, and secure school compounds against unauthorized public 

access. 

Failure to promptly repair broken down or faulty fixtures 

The audit revealed that GES and the MMDAs failed to effectively maintain and repair 

sanitation infrastructure in schools, contrary to the requirements of the Pre-Tertiary 

Education Act, 2020 (Act 1049) and the WASH guidelines. None of the schools visited 

had maintenance plans in place, and although general maintenance manuals existed, 

sanitation infrastructure was not adequately captured in annual plans and budgets. This 

lack of structured maintenance contributed to the deterioration of facilities across 

schools. 

Inspections showed that most toilet facilities had multiple defects, including water 

leakages, broken flushing systems, faulty sinks, damaged doors, and dilapidated 

structures. Only a few schools had facilities without defects, while many others had 

serious structural issues posing safety risks to students. Examples included leaking 

systems, broken fittings, and weakened or collapsed toilet slabs. In some schools, 

facilities were in such poor condition that they required immediate intervention to prevent 

further harm., 

The breakdown of facilities was partly attributed to poor usage practices by pupils and 

students, such as improper use of water closets and disposal of inappropriate materials 

into toilets. However, the prolonged failure to repair these defects meant that many 

facilities remained unusable for long periods. As a result, students were forced to queue 

for the few functional toilets or resort to open defecation, highlighting the severe 

consequences of neglecting maintenance of sanitation infrastructure in schools. 

Management Response 

Management explained that although schools are provided with general maintenance 

guidelines, inadequate budgetary allocations for maintenance, delays in the release of 

/ 10} Page

9.3 

funds, and competing operational priorities limited the ability of schools and MMDAS to 

undertake timely repdirs. Management further noteed that some of the damage resulted 

from misuse and vandalism of facilities by pupils, including the disposal of inappropriate 

materials into toilet Systems, which increased maintenance costs and the frequency of 

breakdowns. 

Responses Given by Management at the Public Hearing 

At the public hearing, Management admitted that the maintenance of sanitation facilities 

had not received the required level of attention due to inadequate funding and the absence 

of dedicated maintehance budgets in many schools. Management explained that priority 

had often been giveh to the construction of new facilities rather than the maintenance of 

existing ones. 

Management inforthed the Committee that the Ghana Education Service has issued 

directives requiring District Directors of Education and Heads of Schools to conduct 

periodic inspectiols of sanitation facilities and report defects promptly. It further 

indicated that arrangements had been made with the MMDAS to undertake emergency 

repairs on facilities that pose health and safety risks. 

Committee Recominendation 

The Committee is concerned that the continued neglect of maintenance has resulted in 

the deterioration of sanitation facilities, exposing pupils to health hazards, compromising 

their dignity, and disrupting effective teaching and learning. 

The Committee therefore recommends that GES, in collaboration with the MMDAs, 

should establish and implement a structured preventive maintenance programme for 

sanitation facilities in all public schools. It is further recommended that the Ministry of 

Education should ensure that annual budgets of schools and District Education 

Directorates include dedicated allocations for the maintenance and repair of sanitation 

infrastructure. 

Ineffective supervision 

The audit found that supervision of school health and sanitation by School Health 

Education Programme (SHEP) Coordinators was inadequate, despite guidelines 

requiring them to visit schools at least twice each term. Although SHEP is mandated to 

monitor health conditions and ensure proper sanitation in schools, the auditors observed 

that these visits wefe either not conducted as required or were ineffective in addressing 

sanitation issues. Consequently, problems such as inadequate, poorly maintained, and 

unclean toilet facilities were not properly identified or reported for corrective action. 

Where visits occurted, reports focused mainly on other health interventions such as 

deworming, nutrition, mosquito net distribution, menstrual hygiene, and oral health, with 

little or no attentiont given to sanitation infrastructure. This gap meant that critical issues 

1M[Page

relating to toilet facilities were overlooked, allowing poor conditions to persist across 

schoals without adequate intervention from the Ghana Education Service. 

Management responses 

Heads of schools especially in the Northern Region explained to the Auditors that 

because of communities’ intrusion in the use of the school toilets, the schools had 

challenges with cleaning the facilities. They further explained that despite engaging the 

communities and locking the facilities, the community members break the locks to use 

the toilet facilities. The heads of schools indicated therefore that they found it difficult to 

assign pupils to clean toilet facilities also used by adults from the communities. Due to 

the failure of both the schools and community members to do the cleaning, school toilets 

were left in unhygienic conditions. 

According to teachers and prefects, the broken-down toilet fixtures were because of poor 

user practices by pupils and students. They explained that students climbed and squatted 

on the WCs instead of sitting on them, leading to the breakdowns. 

The SHEP Coordinators explained that they did not visit schools often as required 

because they did not have the funds or vehicles to effectively carry out monitoring 

activities of the many schools in their jurisdiction. They further explained that they were 

only able to monitor schools during collaborations with donors and development partners 

such as UNICEF, WHO, Plan International, World Vision, Global Communities and 

Water Aid who come with their own cbjectives which does not include monitoring of 

toilet facilities in schools. 

Response given to the Committee at the public hearing 

The Committee was informed that the Goods and Services allocated has been made 

available to the schools and directors have been informed to release resources to the 

SHEP Coordinators to monitor their sanitation situation and report to GES for action, if 

need be. 

It was also disclosed to the Committee that Kumasi Girls High School now has a 20- 

seater toilet facility that is augmenting the existing ones. The one at Presbyterian Boys 

High School, Legon has also been handed over to the school and is in use. 

The Hon Deputy Minister for Education assured the Committee that the rest of the 

uncompleted projects and those complete without sanitary facilities, would be catered for 

in the GET-Fund Formula which was yet to come to Parliament. 

The Hon Deputy Minister shared similar sentiments with the Committee that, 

pupils/students should not be made to clean the sanitary facilities in the schools because 

they can contract bacteria, resulting in disease outbreak like cholera, diarrhoea and the 

rest. 

12|Page

10.0 

Committee Recommendation 

The Committee recommends that the Ministry ensures funds are made available for 

SHEP Coordinators to carry out effective monitoring of health-related issues and 

sanitation in schools and report on them to GES. The Committee further urges the 

Ministry to expedite action on the measures it wants to undertake in order to put the 

sanitary facilities to tise within the shortest possible time. 

CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATION 

Having scrutinised the Performance Audit Report, the Committee observed that MoE and 

GES failed to ensure the adequate provision and accessibility of toilet facilities in public 

schools. The Committee further noted that existing facilities were not properly 

maintained or promptly repaired when faulty, thereby compromising hygiene standards 

and undermining a safe and conducive learning environment for pupils and students. 

In light of the forgoing findings of the audit, the Committce recommends that: 

i. The Ministry of Education, GES and MMDAs should implement a time-bound plan 

to eliminate the toilet deficit in public schools; 

ii. All new school infrastructure should include adequate toilet facilities and reliable 

water supply; 

iii. the Ministry of Education, GES and relevant stakeholders should ensure sustainable 

water supply for all school toilet facilities; 

iv. Completed sanitation projects should promptly be handed over to beneficiary schools; 

v. GES should enforce regular cleaning, maintenance and timely repair of school toilet 

facilities; 

vi. Government should ensure adequate and timely funding for sanitation infrastructure 

and maintenance; 

vii. GES should provide dedicated budgetary support for the maintenance of sanitation 

facilities; 

viil. The Ministry of Education should adequately resource SHEP Coordinators to 

effectively monitor sanitation in schools; 

ix. The Ministry of Education, GES and MMDAs should strengthen sanitation education, 

supervision and prdtection of school toilet facilities; and 

X. The Ministry of Education should periodically report to the Committee on the 

implementation of these recommendations. 

13|Page

Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the House adopts this Report on the 

Performance Audit of the Auditor-General on the Provision and Maintenance of Toilet 

Facilities in Public Schools together with the recommendations contained herein.
