text:
1 

LECTURE BY THE RT. HON. ALBAN SUMANA KINGSFORD 
BAGBIN  

SPEAKER OF PARLIAMENT  
TO MARK THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY CELEBRATION OF THE 

SUPREME COURT 
THURSDAY 23RD JULY 2026 

“THE SUPREME COURT IN THE LIFE OF THE 1992 
CONSTITUTION- TAKING STOCK AND LOOKING FORWARD” 

His Lordship Justice Jones Mawulorm Doste, (rtd) JSC and 
Venerable Chairman for this Lecture 
His Lordships the Chief Justice of Ghana and former Chief Justices 
Hon Attorney General and Minister of Justice  
Your Lordships and Ladyships, Justices of the Supreme Court 
Your Lordships and Ladyships of the Superior Courts of Judicature, 
both serving and retired  
Your Honours and Worships 
Revered King’s,  Queen Mothers, Traditional and Faith Leaders,  
The President, Officers and Members of the Ghana Bar Association 
& Law Society of Ghana  
Members of the Judicial Council 
Members of the Diplomatic Corps 
Civil Society Leaders, Captains of Industry and other Private Sector 
Players  
Distinguished Members of the Legal Academy 
Members of the Media  
Invited Guests 
Ladies and Gentlemen. 

I deem it a great honor and privilege to be invited to deliver a lecture 
to mark the celebration of the 150TH anniversary of the Supreme 
Court of Ghana. I am deeply grateful to His Lordship the Chief 
Justice, the Judicial Service and the Planning Committee for the 
invitation to deliver this Third Anniversary Lecture as part of the 
historic celebration of the Supreme Court of Ghana. 

I receive the invitation not merely as a personal honour, nor solely as 
a courtesy extended to the Parliament of Ghana, but as a recognition 
of the enduring constitutional relationship between two co-equal 

 2 

institutions that stand at the heart of our democratic Republic. 
Parliament and the Judiciary exercise distinct constitutional 
mandates, yet they are united by a common constitutional purpose, 
to uphold the Constitution, preserve the Rule of Law and safeguard 
the democratic aspirations of the people of Ghana. 

A Historic Milestone in Ghana's Constitutional Journey 

Today's celebration marks far more than the passage of one hundred 
and fifty years. It commemorates the remarkable journey of one of 
Ghana's oldest and most enduring public institutions whose 
evolution has been inseparably intertwined with the constitutional, 
political and legal development of our nation. 

Few public institutions in Ghana have endured for one hundred and 
fifty years. Fewer still have remained relevant through successive 
constitutional dispensations, changing systems of government and 
profound political transformation. Established in 1876 by the 
enactment of the Supreme Court Ordinance, during the colonial era, 
the Supreme Court has witnessed the transition from colonial 
administration to independence; from parliamentary government to 
republican governance; through periods of constitutional 
interruption and military rule; and ultimately to the restoration and 
consolidation of constitutional democracy under the Constitution, 
1992. 

Its institutional memory spans almost every defining chapter of 
Ghana's constitutional history. Indeed, the history of the Supreme 
Court mirrors, in many respects, the constitutional history of our 
Republic itself. 

Across changing constitutional orders, evolving political philosophies 
and successive generations of judges, the Court has remained a 
central institution in the administration of justice. While its 
jurisdiction, institutional design and jurisprudence have necessarily 
evolved, its enduring responsibility has remained constant—to 
administer justice according to law and to uphold the constitutional 
order of the State. 

 3 

For that reason, this sesquicentennial is not merely a judicial 
celebration. It is a national milestone. 

The Supreme Court and Ghana's Constitutional Development 

The significance of this anniversary extends well beyond the 
Judiciary. The Rule of Law is not the preserve of judges alone. 
Constitutionalism is not the exclusive concern of lawyers. The 
administration of justice is not merely a judicial enterprise. These are 
national values upon which the peace, stability and democratic 
governance of our Republic depend. 

Every Ghanaian who has exercised the right to vote in peaceful 
elections, every citizen who has sought protection against unlawful 
governmental action, every institution that has discharged its 
constitutional mandate within the framework of law and every 
generation that has witnessed the peaceful transfer of political power 
has, in one way or another, benefited from the work of the Judiciary 
and, ultimately, from the constitutional leadership of the Supreme 
Court. 

The Court has therefore occupied a place that extends beyond the 
courtroom. It has become one of the principal institutions through 
which constitutional democracy has been nurtured, constitutional 
disputes peacefully resolved and public confidence in the Rule of Law 
sustained. 

Its contribution to national development cannot be measured solely 
by the judgments it has delivered. It must also be measured by the 
constitutional stability it has helped to secure and the confidence it 
has inspired in democratic governance. 

Why This Lecture Matters 

Anniversaries of this significance invite more than celebration. They 
invite honest national reflection. 

They require us to look back with gratitude, assess the present with 
intellectual honesty and institutional humility, and look to the future 
with confidence and renewed purpose. 

 4 

The theme assigned for this lecture "The Supreme Court in the Life 
of the 1992 Constitution: Taking Stock and Looking Forward" 
captures that responsibility with admirable precision. 

It invites us to consider the Supreme Court established by Article 
126(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992 not merely 
as an institution of distinguished history, but as a unique living 
constitutional actor whose decisions, jurisprudence and institutional 
leadership have profoundly influenced the operation of the Fourth 
Republic over the past thirty three years. 

Equally, it challenges us to reflect on the future. As Ghana's 
democracy continues to mature, the constitutional questions 
confronting the Court will become increasingly complex. Advances in 
technology, evolving notions of human rights, changing models of 
governance, economic transformation and rising public expectations 
will continue to test the resilience of our constitutional institutions. 

The question before us, therefore, is not simply how the Supreme 
Court has served the Constitution over the past thirty-three years. It 
is how it must continue to serve the Republic and the people in the 
decades yet to come. 

The Central Thesis 

The central thesis of my lecture is straightforward. No institution has 
exercised a greater influence on the practical operation of the 
Constitution, 1992, than the Supreme Court. 

Through its interpretation and enforcement of constitutional 
provisions, the development of constitutional doctrine, the protection 
of fundamental rights and freedoms, the resolution of disputes 
among the organs of State and the articulation of constitutional 
principles, the Court has profoundly shaped the constitutional 
character of the Fourth Republic. 

Its jurisprudence has influenced not only the development of the law 
but also the conduct of public institutions, the expectations of 
citizens and the evolution of Ghana's constitutional culture. 

 5 

Yet constitutional maturity demands more than celebration. No 
doubt a lot has been achieved. Yes. But it is equally a truism that a 
lot is yet to be done. This requires honest reflection. And honest 
reflection I commit to do in this lecture .  

The true strength of a constitutional democracy lies not in the 
unquestioned authority of any single institution, but in the fidelity of 
all constitutional actors to the Constitution itself. The Constitution, 
not Parliament, not the Executive and not the Judiciary, remains 
supreme. The continuing challenge for every arm of State is to 
exercise its constitutional authority in a manner that strengthens, 
rather than disturbs, the constitutional order established by the 
framers of the Constitution. 

It is against that standard that we must take stock of the Supreme 
Court's contribution to our constitutional democracy and consider 
the responsibilities that lie ahead. 

Roadmap of the Lecture 

Accordingly, this lecture proceeds in four substantive Parts. 

First, I shall examine the place of the Supreme Court within the 
constitutional architecture of the Fourth Republic and the pivotal 
role assigned to it under the Constitution. 

Second, I shall take stock of the Court's contribution to Ghana's 
constitutional democracy by examining its jurisprudence, its 
protection of constitutional supremacy and fundamental rights, its 
role in preserving democratic stability, its constitutional dialogue 
with Parliament and the other arms of Government, and the 
institutional challenges that remain. 

Third, I shall offer some reflections on the future of constitutional 
adjudication in Ghana, including the imperative need to preserve the 
Rule of Law, maintain coherence in constitutional interpretation, 
uphold the delicate equilibrium among the arms of Government and 
ensure that the Judiciary continues to command the confidence and 
trust of Ghanaians and the world. 

 6 

Finally, I shall conclude with some reflections on the shared 
constitutional responsibility of all institutions of State to preserve, 
protect and defend the Constitution for present and future 
generations. 

Ladies and Gentlemen, it is with these objectives in mind that I now 
turn to the first substantive question posed by today's theme: 

What place has the Supreme Court occupied in the life of the 
Constitution, 1992, and how has it helped to shape the constitutional 
democracy that Ghanaians have come to cherish? 

THE SUPREME COURT IN THE LIFE OF THE CONSTITUTION 
1992 

The Constitutional Foundation of the Fourth Republic 

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen, the adoption, enactment and 
giving to ourselves this Constitution marked far more than the 
inauguration of another constitutional order. It represented the 
collective determination of the Ghanaian people to break decisively 
with a history of constitutional instability and to establish a 
democratic State founded upon constitutional supremacy, the Rule 
of Law, respect for fundamental human rights, accountable 
governance and the separation of powers. 

Unlike previous constitutional experiments that were interrupted by 
unconstitutional changes of government, this Constitution and the 
Fourth Republic has endured for more than three decades. It has 
become Ghana's longest uninterrupted period of constitutional 
governance since independence. This rare achievement is lost on 
many in Ghana.  

That remarkable achievement cannot be attributed to any single 
institution or individual but to a generation of national leaders. It is 
the product of great sacrifice of many Ghanaians and the continuing 
fidelity of the Republic's constitutional institutions to the 
constitutional compact embodied in the Constitution. 

 7 

Among those institutions, the Supreme Court occupies a position of 
singular constitutional visibility and importance. 

The framers of the Constitution deliberately entrusted the Supreme 
Court with responsibilities that extend beyond those traditionally 
associated with the judicial function. They envisaged a Court that 
would not merely determine disputes between litigants but would 
serve as the principal guardian of the constitutional order itself. 

The Supreme Court was therefore designed to be the only apex court 
of the judicial hierarchy, and as the principal constitutional 
custodian of the Republic. This ended the parallel tracks of the Public 
Tribunal and the Supreme Court in the exercise of criminal 
jurisdiction.  

The Supreme Court as the Guardian of Constitutional Supremacy 

The central organising principle of the Constitution, is the supremacy 
of the Constitution itself. 

Article 1 declares that the sovereignty of Ghana resides in the people 
of Ghana, in whose name and for whose welfare the powers of 
Government are to be exercised in the manner and within the limits 
laid down in the Constitution. Article 1 further proclaims that the 
Constitution is the supreme law of Ghana and that any other law 
found to be inconsistent with it shall, to the extent of the 
inconsistency, be void. 

Constitutional supremacy, however, cannot exist merely as a 
declaration. It requires an ultimate institution capable of giving 
practical effect to that principle. 

That responsibility rests, and I forcefully submit, rightly, with the 
Supreme Court and not any other constitutional or legal creation. 

Under article 2, the Supreme Court is empowered to determine 
whether any enactment or conduct is inconsistent with the 
Constitution. Under article 130, it possesses exclusive original 
jurisdiction in all matters relating to the enforcement or 

 8 

interpretation of the Constitution. Under article 131, it exercises final 
appellate jurisdiction over all superior courts. 

Taken together, these provisions confer upon the Court a 
constitutional responsibility unlike that entrusted to any other 
institution of State. 

Its duty is not merely to interpret the Constitution. Its duty is to 
ensure that the Constitution is obeyed and given effect. 

Every constitutional democracy ultimately depends upon an 
institution capable of ensuring that constitutional limits remain 
meaningful and that every exercise of public power remains subject 
to constitutional scrutiny. 

In Ghana, that institution is, according to the Constitution, the 
Supreme Court. A product of a chequered history. A unique but 
complex Court. It is a constitutional court, a court of first instance, 
a supervisor of other courts, a final appellate court, a review court, 
and as an election court. But all these several types of jurisdiction 
does not make the Supreme Court supreme over all constitutional 
institutions in all matters of the rule of law.  

 

The Supreme Court as the Final Constitutional Arbiter 

The significance of the Supreme Court lies not only in the jurisdiction 
conferred upon it by the Constitution but also in the character of the 
questions it is called upon to determine. 

Constitutional disputes rarely concern private rights alone. They 
frequently involve the distribution of public power, the interpretation 
of, and the application by, constitutional institutions and the 
mediation and reconciliation of competing constitutional values. 

Questions concerning the powers of Parliament, the authority of the 
Executive, the protection of fundamental rights, the conduct of 
elections, the validity of legislation and the interpretation of 

 9 

constitutional procedures ultimately find their way before the 
Supreme Court. 

In resolving such questions, the Court performs a function that 
extends beyond adjudication. It gives practical meaning to the 
Constitution. It defines constitutional boundaries. It clarifies 
institutional responsibilities. It has the opportunity to contribute to 
the development and maintenance of a system of good governance.  

It ensures that constitutional power is exercised only within 
constitutional limits. 

In this sense, every constitutional judgment contributes to the 
continuing life of the Constitution itself. The Court does not merely 
interpret constitutional provisions. It shapes the manner in which 
those provisions operate within the daily life of the Republic. 

The Supreme Court and the Development of Constitutional 
Culture 

The influence of the Supreme Court therefore extends well beyond 
the courtroom. Its decisions shape what constitutional scholars often 
describe as a nation's constitutional culture. 

A Constitution becomes meaningful not merely because it exists as a 
legal document but because citizens, governments and public 
institutions develop confidence that constitutional disputes will be 
resolved peacefully and according to law. 

One of the most remarkable achievements of the Fourth Republic has 
been the gradual emergence of such a constitutional culture. Today, 
constitutional controversies that might once have generated political 
confrontation are increasingly submitted to judicial determination. 

Governments comply with constitutional judgments. Parliament 
adjusts its procedures in response to constitutional interpretation. 

Public institutions increasingly seek constitutional guidance before 
acting. Citizens invoke constitutional rights with growing confidence. 
These developments reflect more than legal progress. 

 10 

They demonstrate the gradual entrenchment of constitutionalism 
within Ghanaian public life. 

The Supreme Court has played a central role in nurturing that 
constitutional culture. By providing authoritative constitutional 
interpretation and peaceful resolution of institutional disputes, it has 
strengthened public confidence that constitutional disagreements 
should be resolved not through political confrontation or extra-
constitutional means but through the institutions established by the 
Constitution itself. 

Perhaps no greater contribution can be made to a constitutional 
democracy. 

The Supreme Court as Constitutional Steward 

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen, 

Every Constitution is intended to endure. Yet no Constitution can 
anticipate every challenge that future generations will encounter. 

The framers of the Constitution, 1992, understood this reality. They 
established enduring constitutional principles while entrusting 
future generations and particularly the Judiciary with the 
responsibility of ensuring that those principles remain capable of 
guiding an evolving democratic society. 

In that sense, the Supreme Court performs a role that may properly 
be described as constitutional stewardship. 

It must remain faithful to the text of the Constitution while ensuring 
that its provisions continue to serve the broader constitutional values 
for which the Constitution was adopted. 

It must preserve constitutional continuity without resisting 
legitimate constitutional evolution. It must safeguard constitutional 
certainty while ensuring that the law remains responsive to changing 
circumstances. 

This is no easy responsibility. 

 11 

It demands legal scholarship, institutional wisdom, constitutional 
restraint, cool heads, and, above all, an unwavering fidelity to the 
Constitution. For the Supreme Court's authority ultimately derives 
not from the power to pronounce the law but from the confidence of 
the Ghanaian people that its judgments faithfully reflect the 
Constitution and strengthen the democratic order established in 
their name. It should never be lost to any person, that the power of 
the Supreme Court to interpret and to enforce the provisions of the 
Constitution, emanate from the people. It is a delegated power.  

It is against this constitutional mandate that the work of the 
Supreme Court over the past three decades must be assessed. 

Accordingly, having considered the constitutional role assigned to the 
Supreme Court under the Constitution, I now turn to the central 
evaluative task posed by today's theme to take stock of the Court's 
contribution to Ghana's constitutional democracy, to acknowledge its 
achievements, to reflect upon the challenges that remain, and to 
consider the lessons that may guide its future. 

TAKING STOCK: THE SUPREME COURT'S CONTRIBUTION TO 
CONSTITUTIONAL DEMOCRACY 

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen, 

Having reflected upon the constitutional place assigned to the 
Supreme Court under the Constitution, it is now appropriate to 
undertake the exercise contemplated by today's theme, to take stock. 

To take stock is neither to celebrate uncritically nor to criticize 
unfairly. It is to assess an institution honestly, recognising its 
achievements, acknowledging its challenges and considering how it 
may continue to strengthen the constitutional order entrusted to its 
care. 

Such reflection is particularly appropriate for an institution that has 
stood at the apex of Ghana's judicial system for many of the one 
hundred and fifty years and has occupied a central place in the 
constitutional life of the Fourth Republic for more than three 
decades. 

 12 

The true measure of the Supreme Court's contribution cannot be 
found simply in the number of constitutional cases it has determined 
or the volume of reported decisions. Rather, it lies in the extent to 
which its jurisprudence has strengthened constitutional government, 
reinforced the Rule of Law, protected individual liberty, preserved 
democratic stability and inspired public confidence in the 
Constitution itself. 

Measured against those constitutional benchmarks, the Supreme 
Court has made an enduring contribution to the success of the 
Fourth Republic. 

Guardian of Constitutional Supremacy 

Perhaps the Court's most significant contribution has been its 
steadfast affirmation that the Constitution remains the supreme law 
of the Republic. 

Constitutional supremacy is the cornerstone upon which every 
democratic institution rests. Without an independent institution 
prepared to enforce constitutional limitations, the supremacy of the 
Constitution would remain little more than an aspirational 
declaration. 

Through its original jurisdiction under articles 2 and 130, the 
Supreme Court has repeatedly demonstrated that constitutional 
authority must prevail over political convenience. 

Landmark decisions such as New Patriotic Party v Attorney-
General (31st December Case), Justice Abdulai v Attorney-
General, and Professor Appiagyei-Atua v Attorney-General have 
become enduring pillars of Ghana's constitutional jurisprudence. 
Collectively, they affirm a fundamental constitutional proposition—
that neither Parliament, nor the Executive, nor any public authority 
exercises power beyond the limits imposed by the Constitution. 

By insisting that constitutional power must always remain subject to 
constitutional restraint, the Court has transformed constitutional 
supremacy from a textual declaration into an operational principle of 
democratic governance. 

 13 

Custodian of Constitutional Equilibrium  

The Supreme Court has also performed an indispensable role in 
preserving the constitutional order established by the framers of the 
Constitution. 

The genius of the Constitution, lies not merely in its separation of 
powers but in its delicate balancing of those powers. Parliament 
legislates. The Executive President governs. The Judiciary interprets 
and enforces the Constitution. 

Each institution derives its authority from the same constitutional 
source. Each is independent in the performance of its constitutional 
mandate. None is supreme over the Constitution. 

Throughout the life of the Fourth Republic, the Supreme Court has 
repeatedly been invited to define the constitutional boundaries 
separating these institutions. 

Its decisions in J.H. Mensah v Attorney-General, Professor 
Stephen Kwaku Asare v Attorney-General, Ezuame Mannan v 
Attorney-General, and other important constitutional cases have 
clarified institutional responsibilities and strengthened 
constitutional accountability. In doing so, the Court has helped 
preserve the constitutional architecture upon which democratic 
governance is anchored in Ghana. 

Protector of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms 

Equally significant has been the Court's contribution to the 
protection of the fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed under 
Chapter Five of the Constitution. 

Constitutions ultimately exist for people. Their legitimacy depends 
not only upon the organisation of public power but also upon the 
protection of human dignity. 

The Supreme Court has, over the years, progressively developed a 
rights-centred constitutional jurisprudence. 

 14 

Through decisions such as New Patriotic Party v Inspector-
General of Police, Ahumah-Ocansey v Electoral 
Commission, Centre for Human Rights & Civil Liberties v 
Attorney-General, Awuni v West African Examinations Council, 
and Martin Kpebu, the Court has reinforced the principle that 
constitutional rights are not merely declaratory ideals but 
enforceable legal guarantees. 

In doing so, it has strengthened public confidence that liberty 
remains protected by an independent Judiciary. 

Anchor of Democratic Stability 

Perhaps nowhere has the Supreme Court's constitutional 
significance been more evident than during periods of political 
contestation. Every constitutional democracy is ultimately tested not 
during periods of consensus but during moments of disagreement. 

Ghana has experienced such moments. Yet one of the defining 
characteristics of the Fourth Republic has been the willingness of 
political actors to submit, even the most contentious constitutional 
disputes, to judicial determination. 

The 2012 Presidential Election Petition remains perhaps the 
clearest demonstration of this constitutional maturity. Regardless of 
differing political opinions regarding the outcome, the proceedings 
demonstrated that constitutional controversies of the highest 
political significance could be resolved peacefully within the 
framework of the law. 

That remains one of the great constitutional achievements of the 
Fourth Republic. We owe the Supreme Court a debt of gratitude for 
saving our constitutional democracy.  

Parliament and the Judiciary: Constitutional Dialogue Between 
Co-equal Institutions 

Perhaps no constitutional relationship better illustrates the 
maturation of Ghana's constitutional democracy than the evolving 
relationship between Parliament and the Supreme Court. 

 15 

The Fourth Republic has witnessed an increasing number of 
constitutional disputes involving parliamentary proceedings, 
legislative enactments and the exercise of parliamentary authority. 
This development should not be regarded as evidence of institutional 
conflict. Rather, it reflects the natural consequence of a 
constitutional order founded upon constitutional supremacy and 
judicial review. 

Through its decisions, the Supreme Court has clarified the 
constitutional limits of legislative authority, interpreted 
parliamentary procedures, examined the scope of parliamentary 
privilege and reinforced the principle that every constitutional 
institution—including Parliament itself—remains subject to the 
Constitution. 

These decisions have not always escaped criticism within Parliament 
or the wider constitutional community. Nor should one expect them 
to. Constitutional adjudication frequently requires courts to 
determine difficult questions upon which reasonable constitutional 
actors may legitimately disagree. 

Such disagreement is neither unusual nor unhealthy. Indeed, it is 
often the hallmark of a vibrant constitutional democracy. 

The true measure of constitutional maturity is not the absence of 
institutional disagreement but the ability of constitutional 
institutions to resolve those disagreements through lawful due 
processes, mutual respect and fidelity to the Constitution. 

Parliament and the Judiciary derive their legitimacy from different 
constitutional sources. Parliament speaks with the democratic 
mandate of the electorate. The Judiciary speaks with the authority of 
the Constitution. Neither source of legitimacy diminishes the other. 
Rather, both are indispensable to the preservation of constitutional 
democracy, since both emanate from the same source, the people of 
Ghana.  

Accordingly, judicial review should continue to be exercised with due 
regard for Parliament's constitutional role as the representative 
institution of the sovereign people, just as Parliament must continue 

 16 

to respect the Judiciary's exclusive responsibility to interpret and 
enforce the Constitution. Both are called upon to uphold, preserve, 
protect and defend the Constitution.  

Institutional comity is not constitutional deference. It is the 
disciplined recognition that constitutional government flourishes 
when each arm of Government faithfully performs its own 
constitutional responsibilities while respecting the constitutional 
competence of the others. 

Institutional Renewal: The Challenges of Constitutional 
Stewardship 

Taking stock also requires intellectual honesty. No constitutional 
institution, however distinguished, can rely upon its history alone. 

Every generation renews public confidence in constitutional 
institutions through its own conduct. The Supreme Court is no 
exception. 

The increasing complexity of constitutional litigation, the growing 
demand for timely justice, the need for greater accessibility, the 
importance of coherent constitutional jurisprudence and the 
expectations of a technologically sophisticated society all present new 
institutional challenges. 

These are not uniquely Ghanaian concerns. They confront 
constitutional courts throughout the democratic world. 

The distinguishing characteristic of great constitutional courts is not 
that they avoid such challenges but that they confront them with 
openness, wisdom, courage and a continuing commitment to 
institutional renewal. 

An Enduring Constitutional Legacy 

As we take stock of the Supreme Court's contribution to the life of 
the Constitution, 1992, one conclusion emerges with unmistakable 
clarity. 

 17 

The Supreme Court has been one of the principal architects of 
Ghana's constitutional democracy. Through its jurisprudence, it has 
strengthened constitutional supremacy, protected fundamental 
rights, preserved democratic stability, clarified the relationships 
among the organs of State and reinforced public confidence in 
constitutional government. 

These achievements deserve recognition. But they also carry an 
enduring responsibility. 

For every generation inherits constitutional institutions from those 
who came before. 

The measure of faithful stewardship is whether those institutions are 
handed to the next generation stronger than they were received. 

It is against that responsibility that we must now consider the future. 
For the question before us is no longer simply what the Supreme 
Court has achieved. 

The more important question is what the Republic will require of the 
Supreme Court in the decades ahead. It is to that future and to the 
constitutional responsibilities that accompany it that I now turn.  

LOOKING FORWARD: THE SUPREME COURT AND THE FUTURE 
OF CONSTITUTIONAL DEMOCRACY 

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen, 

Every significant constitutional anniversary is both a celebration of 
achievement and an invitation to renewal. It challenges an institution 
not merely to reflect upon its past, but to prepare itself for the 
constitutional demands of the future. 

The Republic that the Supreme Court will serve over the coming 
decades will be markedly different from the Republic that emerged in 
January 1993. 

The constitutional questions of tomorrow will increasingly arise from 
technological innovation, artificial intelligence, digital governance, 

 18 

cyber security, data protection, biotechnology, environmental justice, 
climate change, regional economic integration, cross-border 
commerce and rapidly evolving conceptions of individual rights and 
governmental responsibility. 

The Court will be called upon to resolve questions that the framers 
of the Constitution could scarcely have anticipated. 

Yet while the issues confronting the Court will inevitably change, its 
constitutional mission must remain constant. 

The Supreme Court exists to uphold the supremacy of the 
Constitution. 

It exists to safeguard the Rule of Law. 

It exists to truly and faithfully administer justice impartially without 
fear or favour, affection or ill-will.  

It exists to preserve the constitutional order upon which democratic 
governance depends. 

Those responsibilities remain timeless and sacred. The greatest 
tribute we can pay those who built this institution is not simply to 
celebrate its history but to leave it stronger than we found it – more 
independent, more accessible, more transparent and more 
intellectually rigorous. May the next one hundred and fifty years 
produce a Supreme Court admired not merely because its decisions 
are final, but because it’s reasoning is principled, its processes 
inspire confidence, and every Ghanaian, regardless of status or 
political persuasion, approaches its doors with the quiet assurance 
that justice will be done according to law.  

Independence, impartiality, and Constitutional Accountability 

The enduring strength of the Supreme Court rests first and foremost 
upon its independence, impartiality, diligence and application to 
duty. 

 19 

Independence of the Supreme Court, notwithstanding what other 
players may say, remains one of the greatest constitutional 
achievements of the Constitution. Without an independent Supreme 
Court, constitutional supremacy would become vulnerable, 
fundamental rights insecure and democratic governance uncertain. I 
pray that the Supreme Court of Ghana will continue to demonstrate 
the qualities that have made it a venerable and revered national 
arbiter. The Court should persevere in upholding the rule of law. That 
will be its priceless contribution to Ghana’s development.  

Independence, however, is not an end in itself. Its constitutional 
purpose is to enable judges to decide cases according to law, free 
from improper influence, external pressure or political expediency. 

Independence must therefore always be accompanied by an equally 
profound fidelity to constitutional principle. Not only the Court or the 
Judiciary, but each and every one of us. The culture of 
constitutionalism must be cultivated by all of us. The confidence of 
the people is the Judiciary's greatest institutional asset. That 
confidence cannot simply be assumed because judicial authority is 
constitutionally guaranteed.  

It must continually be earned, earned through integrity, through 
impartiality. through consistency and through intellectual rigour of 
both the institution and the people serving in it. 

Above all, it is earned through judgments that persuade by the force 
of constitutional reasoning and benefits to reinforce public 
confidence that justice has been administered according to law. 

Avoiding the Twin Dangers 

As the Court looks to the future, it must remain vigilant against two 
constitutional dangers. 

The first is constitutional overextension. 

The Constitution entrusts enormous authority to the Supreme Court. 
Jurisdictionally, the Supreme Court exercises an exceptionally broad 
and multifaceted jurisdiction. The Court must resist the temptation 

 20 

to extend its jurisdictionally powers to matters that might be 
considered as constitutional overextension. The authority of the 
Court must always be exercised with constitutional discipline. Courts 
strengthen democracy not by assuming responsibilities entrusted to 
the political branches, but by ensuring that every institution 
faithfully performs the responsibilities assigned to it by the 
Constitution. My humble submission is for the Supreme Court to 
deploy its powers in ways which make the law serve the purpose of 
society.  

The temptation to substitute judicial preference for constitutional 
command must always be resisted. 

The second danger is excessive judicial restraint.  

There will be moments when constitutional rights are threatened, 
constitutional limits disregarded or democratic institutions placed 
under strain. At such moments, excessive restraint may prove as 
damaging to constitutional democracy as excessive intervention. In 
the same way the Supreme Court should “restrain itself from 
expanding its jurisdiction by interpretation to cover more and more 
non-Strategic cases. Its case load needs to be limited so that it can 
be more effective and able to concentrate on the leading strategic 
legal issues affecting national life”.  

The Constitution expects the Supreme Court to act neither timidly 
nor aggressively. It expects the Court to act constitutionally. 

The enduring authority of the Supreme Court will therefore lie in its 
ability to avoid both extremes while remaining unwavering in its 
fidelity to the Constitution. 

The Need for Jurisprudential Coherence 

Closely connected to this responsibility is the continuing need for 
coherence in constitutional interpretation. 

The authority of the Supreme Court derives not merely from the 
finality of its judgments but from the quality, coherence and 
predictability of its constitutional reasoning. 

 21 

Constitutional adjudication must provide clarity where uncertainty 
exists, certainty where ambiguity persists and principled guidance 
where public institutions seek constitutional direction. Citizens, 
Parliament, the Executive, investors and the wider society organise 
their affairs upon the reasonable expectation that constitutional 
principles will be interpreted consistently and applied predictably. 

In this regard, one of the continuing tasks before the Court is the 
development of a coherent philosophy of constitutional 
interpretation. 

Over the years, the Court's jurisprudence has, at different times, 
drawn upon both textualism and purposivism or functionalism in 
interpreting constitutional provisions. Neither approach is inherently 
objectionable. Each serves an important function in constitutional 
adjudication. Textualism reminds us that judges must remain 
faithful to the language adopted by the people in their Constitution. 
Purposivism reminds us that constitutional provisions must also be 
interpreted in light of the broader values, objectives and aspirations 
that the Constitution was intended to secure. 

The challenge, however, is not the legitimacy of either methodology. 
The challenge is ensuring principled consistency in determining 
when each approach is appropriately employed. 

Where constitutional interpretation appears to oscillate 
unpredictably between textualism and purposivism without a clearly 
articulated jurisprudential framework, uncertainty may arise in the 
law. Such uncertainty affects not only litigants before the Court but 
also Parliament, the Executive and every public institution that must 
order its affairs in accordance with the Constitution. 

The continued development of a coherent interpretative 
methodology—transparent, principled and firmly anchored in the 
Constitution—will therefore remain one of the Supreme Court's most 
important responsibilities in the years ahead. 

For the Rule of Law requires not only that justice be done, but that 
constitutional reasoning itself be sufficiently coherent, principled and 
predictable to command public confidence. 

 22 

Preserving Constitutional Equilibrium 

Ladies and Gentlemen, perhaps the greatest constitutional 
responsibility awaiting the Supreme Court is the preservation of the 
delicate balance established by the framers of the Constitution and 
the smooth, harmonious transformation of the balance to 
equilibrium of the partners of governance . 

The Constitution deliberately distributes public power among three 
independent arms. Parliament legislates. The Executive President 
governs. The Judiciary interprets and enforces the Constitution. 
Each institution derives its authority from the same constitutional 
source. 

Each possesses democratic legitimacy appropriate to its 
constitutional function. Each serves the same sovereign people. 

The success of Ghana's constitutional democracy has depended not 
upon the dominance of any one institution but upon the disciplined 
observance of constitutional boundaries by all. This must reflect 
unambiguously in the text of the Constitution.  

As constitutional disputes inevitably arise, the Court will continue to 
play the indispensable role of constitutional umpire. 

In performing that role, judicial review should always be exercised 
with full appreciation of the constitutional functions, democratic 
legitimacy and institutional competence of the other arms of 
Governance . 

Again, let me reemphasise that Institutional comity does not require 
constitutional deference. Nor does it diminish judicial independence. 

Rather, it reflects the recognition that constitutional governance 
flourishes when every institution exercises its powers with restraint, 
mutual respect and fidelity to the Constitution. The Judiciary, 
Parliament and the Executive are not constitutional rivals. They are 
constitutional partners in the service of the Republic. 

A CONSTITUTIONAL CHARGE TO THE SUPREME COURT 

 23 

Permit me, therefore, to conclude this forward-looking reflection with 
a respectful constitutional charge to the Supreme Court. 

As you embark upon your next one hundred and fifty years of service, 
uphold the Rule of Law with courage and unwavering fidelity. 

Defend the supremacy of the Constitution without fear or favour. 
Ensure that judicial independence is captured in the text of the 
Constitution and matched by judicial excellence, consistency and 
accountability to constitutional principle. 

Develop a jurisprudence that is intellectually rigorous, coherent and 
accessible, one that provides certainty to citizens, guidance to public 
institutions and confidence to future generations. 

Conform with a clear and deliberate intent to transform the delicate 
constitutional balance that has enabled the Fourth Republic to 
become Ghana's longest period of uninterrupted constitutional 
government to constitutional equilibrium with the other partners in 
Governance . 

Remember that every constitutional judgment speaks beyond the 
immediate parties before the Court. Every judgment either 
strengthens or weakens public confidence in constitutional 
governance. Every judgment contributes to the constitutional culture 
that future generations will inherit.  

Above all, ensure that every decision of the Supreme Court leaves the 
Constitution stronger than the Court found it. 

History will not judge this great institution merely by the number of 
judgments it has delivered or the distinction of those who have 
adorned its Bench. 

History will judge it by whether, when constitutional principle was 
tested, it remained faithful to the Constitution, whether, when the 
Rule of Law was challenged, it stood firm and whether, through its 
jurisprudence, it secured for future generations an enduring 
constitutional democracy founded upon Ghana’s motto, freedom and 
justice. And more importantly, the true measure of the Supreme 

 24 

Court ‘s greatness will not simply be the quality of it’s judgements, 
but the confidence every Ghanaian has that justice will be done 
according to law. 

If the first one hundred and fifty years established the Supreme Court 
as one of the great institutions of our Republic, may the next one 
hundred and fifty years establish it among the world's most respected 
supreme courts, an institution whose jurisprudence continues to 
illuminate the path of constitutionalism, deepen public confidence in 
the administration of justice and secure the democratic future of the 
Republic of Ghana. 

Congratulations to the Supreme Court of Ghana on one hundred and 
fifty years of distinguished service to the nation. May its next century 
and a half be marked by unwavering dedication to the Republic of 
Ghana. 

I thank you for your kind attention.

INTRODUCTION 

The Committee on Lands and Natural Resources considered the Annual Statement by the 

Audit Committee of the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands covering the period 

January to December 2024. The Committee met to review the findings, assess the level o
f 

compliance with audit recommendations, and deliberate on key issues that emerged from
 

the report presented by the Audit Commitiee. 

The consideration forms part of the oversight mandate of the Committee in ensuring sound 

financial management, adherence to audit standards and accountability in the operati
ons of 

the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands in pursuant of Order 240 of the Standing 

Orders of Parliament. 

The Deputy Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, officials from the Ministry of
 Lands 

and Natural Resources as well as officials from the Office of the Administrator of School 

Lands attended upon the Committee during the consideration of the Annual 
Statement by 

the Audit Committee of the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands for the Year 2024.

). 

BACKGROUND 

The Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands is mandated to mana
ge public lands, 

optimize revenue from land assets, and ensure proper stewardship of l
and resources in 

accordance with national laws and regulations. 

The Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921) provides, amongst others, t
hat the

implementation of recommendations contained in the Internal Audit Report, External 

Audit Report, Parliament’s decision on the Auditor-General’s Report, and the Auditor- 

General’s Management Letter. This Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of the 

Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands for the Year 2024 was therefore submitted in 

compliance with the provisions of the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921). 

AUDIT OBJECTIVES AND SCOPE 

The audit sought to evaluate: 

. The validity and completeness of payroll and staff validation systems. 

. Timeliness and accuracy of withholding tax payments, 

. Asset management practices, including tagging and accounting for fixed assets. 

. Revenue collection and bank remittances. 

. Measures to prevent encroachment and ensure proper land use. 

. Operational challenges and mitigation measures. 

Internal Control 

The Audit Committee advised management on the following to improve Internal Controls: 

i Supervision of Revenue Collectors to reduce financial shortages in the Districts and 

Regional Offices. 

ii. Frequent audit to be conducted at revenue shortage Districts and Regional Offices. 

iid. Development of draft Risk Register and Policy for OASL. 

iv. The Accounts Directorate should also embark on financial monitoring exercise. 

Consideration of the Audit Statement 

The Audit Committee presented the major findings of the 2024 Audit Statement and the 

actions taken by management to address them, The following are the key issues considered 

" by the Committee. 

Validation of Officers 

The Audit Commitiee reported that some officers were not validated by the Office of the 

Administrator of Stool Lands due to delays in enrolling their details on the electronic 

payment voucher system of the Controller and Accountant-General. The Committee 

recommended that the Principal Spending Officer and the Head of Human Resource ensure 

that all affected officers are immediately validated to regularise their payroll status. This 

recommendation was fully implemented. The affocted officers have been placed on the 

appropriate payrolls and redeployed accordingly.

Withholding Taxes 

Delays were recorded in the payment of withholding taxes amounting to thirty-two 

thousand eight hundred and six Ghana cedis. The Audit Committee advised management 

{0 ensure the payment of all outstanding amounts to the Ghana Revenue Authority and to 

strengthen internal controls to prevent a recurrence. Management confirmed that the entire 

amount has been paid and that the necessary receipts have been verified by the Internal 

Audit Unit. 

Non-Embossment of Fixed Assets 

The report revealed that some fixed assets were not embossed and recorded properly. The 

Audit Commitiee directed that all assets be tagged with unique identification numbers to 

enhance tracking and accountability. 

The Committee noted that this directive has been complied with as all assets have been 

embossed and inventoried by the Estate Unit. 

Unaccounted Revenue 

An amount of Seven Thousand, Seven Hundred and Forty Ghana Cedis (GHS7,740) was 

reported as unaccounted for. The Audit Committce instructed that the amount be recovered 

and paid into the designated bank account of the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands. 

The Commitice was informed that the entire amount has been recovered from the 

responsible officers and deposited into the official account. 

Encroachment on Lands 

The report indicated instances of encroachment on lands belonging to the Office of the 

Administrator of Stool Lands in the Northern Region. The Audit Committee recommended 

the fencing of the affected lands and the development of a comprehensive land 

" management plan to prevent further encroachment. Management informed the Committee 

that funds have been carmarked in the 2025 budget and procurement plan has been made 

for the construction of a perimeter wall. 

Absence of Designated Driver in the Upper East Region 

The absence of a designated driver in the Upper East Region created operational 

challenges. The Audit Committec recommended that temporary arrangements be made to 

ensure mobility for official duties. The Committee was informed that a driver has been 

assigned to the region through the Regional Coordinating Council.

Unearned Salaries 

The Committee examined instances of unearned salaries in the Ashanti, Bono, and 

Northern Regions. It was established that an officer had travelled outside the country while 

still on the payroll. Management confirmed that the unearned salaries have been recovered 

and evidence of repayment submitted to the Audit Unit. 

Control of Revenue Collection 

The Committee expressed concern about delays in banking revenue and weak internal 

control measures. Management explained that officers in remote areas faced challenges 

accessing banking facilities, hence delays occurred. To address this, a mobile money 

payment system has been introduced to facilitate timely transfers into the main account of 

the Office. 

Tt was reported that with the support of the Audit Committee, management implemented 

the audit recommendation which lead to the reirieval of a total amount of Sixty-One 

Thousand, Three Hundred and Ninety Ghana Cedis (GHg¢61,390.00) being IGF collected 

which hitherto was not banked and therefore not accounted for. Details are as follows:

Delayed Budget Releases 

The Committee noted with concern that the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands had 

. received only *wo months of releases from the Minerals Development Fund, with seven 

months in arrears. Management stated that correspondence has been initiated with the Fund 

and the Ministry of Finance to ensure the immediate release of the outstanding amounts. 

Observations and Recommendations 

The Committee on Lands and Natural Resources observed that management of the Office 

of the Administrator of Stool Lands has made significant progress in implementing the 

recommendations contained in the 2024 Audit Statement. The payment of outstanding 

withholding taxes and the tagging of fixed assets have been completed in accordance with 

the directives of the Audit Committee.

The Committee further noted that certain weaknesses still exist in the internal control 

systems, particularly in the area of revenue collection and reconciliation of Duplicate 

Carbon Receipts. It was recommended that management should strengthen oversight and 

ensure that no new receipt books are issued until previous ones have been fully accounted 

for and certified. 

The Committee expressed concern about the continued encroachment of lands under the 

cate of the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands. The Committee advised that 

immediate protective measures such as tree planting, the erection of temporary fencing, 

and the placement of site attendants should be considered as cost-effective options pending 

the construction of permanent fence walls. 

In relation to revenue mobilisation, the Committee commended management for 

introducing the mobile money initiative to improve the timeliness of banking, particularly 

in remote areas where access to financial institutions remain limited. Tt was recommended 

that this initiative be fully implemented and closely monitored to prevent revenue leakages 

and enhance accountability. 

The Committee also observed that delays in the release of funds from the Minerals 

Development Fund continue to affect the operations of the Office. Members of the 

Commitice on Lands and Natural Resources urged the Ministry of Lands and Natural
 

Resources to engage the relevant authorities to facilitate timely disbursement of mineral
 

royalty funds to support effective implementation of programmes and projects by 

beneficiary agencies. 

On the issue of missing Duplicate Carbon Receipts, the Committee acknowledged the steps
 

taken by management to report the maiter to the Police and the Economic and Organised
 

Crime Office for investigation. T was recommended that stricter measures be enforced to
 

ensure full accountability by officers responsible for the custody and issuance of
 receipt 

books. 

Finally, the Committee emphasised the need to uphold Article 267 of the Const
itution 

which assigns the collection and management of stool land revenues and royalties
 to the 

Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands. Tt was observed that strict adherence to. this 

constitutional provision would enhance the financial independence of the Office
 of the 

Administrator of Stoo! Lands and ensure that funds are disbursed to the rightful 

beneficiaries without undue delay. 

Page 6 of 7

7.0  CONCLUSION 

The Committee recognizes the efforts made by the Office of the Administrator of School 

Lands in addressing previous irregularities and improving internal controls. However, 

persistent challenges around funding delays, encroachments, and operational constraints 

require ongoing attention. 

The Committee recommends that Parliament adopt this report and support necessary 

reforms and funding to strengthen land administration and safeguard national land 

resources effectively.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON ENERGY ON THE 
ANNUAL STATEMENT BY THE AUDIT COMMITTEE 
OF THE GHANA NATIONAL GAS LIMITED COMPANY 

(GNGLC) FOR THE YEAR 2025 

1.0 INTRODUCTION 

The Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of the Ghana National 

Gas Limited Company for the period January to December 2025 was 

presented to Parliament on 16% June, 2026. 

In accordance with article 103 of the 1992 Constitution and Order 252 of 

the Standing Orders of Parliament, the Statement was referred to the 

Committee on Energy for consideration and report. 

The Committee met and considered the Statement with the Chief Executive 

Officer, Ms. Judith Adjobah Blay and a team of other officials from the Ghana 

National Gas Limited Company. 

The Committee is grateful to the Chief Executive Officer and the team of 

officials from the Ghana National Gas Limited Company for attending upon 

and assisting the Committee in the deliberations on the Annual Statement.

2.0 BACKGROUND 

Ghana National Gas Limited Company (GNGLC) is Ghana’s premiere mid- 

stream gas business company that owns and operates infrastructure 

required for the gathering, processing, transporting and marketing of 

natural gas resources locally and internationally, 

The company supplies gas to the energy and industrial sectors of Ghana. 

The Company’s operations directly influence national power generation, 

" industrial productivity, gas monetisation and revenue mobilisation. 

3.0 

The Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of the Ghana National Gas 

Limited Company for the period January to December 2025 was presented 

to Parliament in accordance with Public Financial Management Act, 2016 

(Act 921). The Statement outlines deficiencies in financial management, 

internal controls, project execution, documentation processes and 

governance structures. These were reviewed alongside the status of 

implementation and management explanations of the various issues raised 

in internal and external auditors reports in respect of the Company for the 

period under review. 

SCOPE OF THE ANNUAL STATEMENT 

The Statement focused on: 

1. Effectiveness of internal controls and compliance standards. 

2. Adequacy and reliability of financial reporting and documentation. 

3. Procurement and contract management practices. 

4, Integrity of revenue assurance systems and opcrational controls, 

5 Governance  performance and  responsiveness to  audit 

recommendations. 

6. Status of action taken on prior audit findings and observations.

4.0 OBSERVATIONS 

4.1 Faulty Warehouse Equipment 

4.2 

The Statement disclosed that the Company’s warchouse backup generator 

had experienced intermittent performance challenges and had not 

consistently met operational requirements although it was subjected to 

routine maintenance. Also, the warchouse roller shutter was defective, 

thereby affecting the efficient operation and security of the warehouse. 

Management informed the Committee that the challenges affecting the 

backup generator had been resolved. It further indicated that procurement 

and fabrication processes were underway to repair and restore the defective 

roller shutter, 

The Committee commends Management for resolving the issues with the 

back-up generator and urges the company to expedite the procurement and 

fabrication processes to ensure the timely restoration of the warehouse roller 

shutter. 

The Committee further recommends that Management strengthens the 

maintenance regime and undertake periodic inspections of critical 

warehouse infrastructure and equipment to minimise operational 

disruptions and safeguard organisational assets. 

Misclassification of Property, Plant and Equipment 

The Statement disclosed that an HVAC system valued at GHS4.7 million and 

a UPS system valued at GHSS.1 million, both acquired during the period 

under review, had not been installed at the time of the audit. As a result, the 

assets were not appropriately reflected in the financial records. 

Management informed the Committee that the installation of both systems 

had since been completed. 

4.3 

While acknowledging the corrective action taken, the Committee notes that 

the issue could have been avoided through stronger planning and oversight. 

The Committee thercfore urges Management to strengthen internal controls 

and improve supervision over the acquisition, installation, and recording of 

capital assets to avoid similar audit findings in the future. 

Review of Useful Life Assessment 

The Audit Committee reported that some Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE) 

had remained in the Fixed Assets Register even though they had been fully 

depreciated, without a reassessment of their useful lives and residual values. 

The Statement observed that where such assets are still in active use, failing 

to review their values periodically may cause the financial statements to not 

fully reflect their current economic value and level of utilisation. 

Management explained that a comprehensive review of the useful lives and 

residual values of all relevant PPE currently in use is underway. The purpose 

of the comprehensive review exercise is to ensure that depreciation charges 

more accurately reflect how the economic benefits of the assets are being 

consumed, in line with applicable accounting standards. 

The Committee encourages Management to ensure the timely completion of 

the review process. Also, there should be regular reassessments of the useful 

lives and residual values of PPE to support accurate and reliable financial 

reporting. 

4.4 Inaccurate Exchange Rates applied to Foreign Currency Tran
slations 

The Statement observed that inaccurate exchange rates had been applied i
n 

translating certain foreign currency transactions and balances, resulting in 

variances between the recorded rates and the official Bank of Ghana 

exchange rates. This exposed the Company to avoidable foreign exchang
e 

losses and increased the risk of material misstatements in the financia
l 

statements,

5.0 

Management explained to the Committee that the variances arose from 

exchange rates applied by foreign suppliers during the settlement of 

transactions. 

The Committee admonished Management to exercise stronger controls to 

ensure that contractual negotiations with suppliers accurately reflect the 

official Bank of Ghana exchange rates. 

The Committee further urges Management to engage the Bank of Ghana to 

explore appropriate arrangements for foreign currency payments to 

suppliers with the aim of minimising exchange rate losses and enhancing 

the accuracy of financial reporting. 

CONCLUSION 

The Committee acknowledges the efforts of Management of the Ghana 

National Gas Company Limited to address the issues raised and implement 

corrective measures to strengthen the Company's operational efficiency, 

financial management and governance systems. The efforts need to be 

sustained to ensure that all outstanding issues are fully and successfully 

resolved. 

The Committee accordingly recommends to the House to adopt this report 

on the Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of the Ghana National 

Gas Company Limited for the year ended 31st December 2025, 

Respectfully submitted. 

X LOUIS YIADOM BOA 

CHAIRMAN, COMMITTEE ON ENERGY CLERK TO THE COMMITTEE 

20 July 2026

IN THE SECOND SESSION OF THE NINTH

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON ENERGY ON 

THE ANNUAL STATEMENT BY THE AUDIT 

COMMITTEE OF NATIONAL PETROLEUM 

AUTHORITY FOR THE YEAR 2024 

1.0 INTRODUCTION 

The Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of National 

Petroleum Authority for the year 2024 was presented to Parliament on 

10% July, 2025 in accordance with Section 88 of the Public Financial 

Management Act, 2016 (Act 921). 

Pursuant to article 103 of the 1992 Constitution and Order 252 of the 

Standing Orders of Parliament, the report was referred to the Committee 

of Energy for consideration and report. 

The Committee met and considered the Statement with a team of officials 

from National Petroleum Authority (NPA). 

The Committee is grateful to the team of officials from NPA for attending 

upon and assisting the Committee during the deliberations on the Annual 

Statement.

PARLIAMENT HOUSE 
OSL - ACCRA 

2.0 BACKGROUND 

The National Petroleum Authority (NPA) is established by the National 

Petroleum Authority Act, 2005 (Act 691) and mandated to regulate Ghana's 

downstream petroleum industry. The Authority has responsibility for 

ensuring safe, efficient, competitive, transparent, and consumer- 

focused downstream petroleum operations in the country. 

The Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of the National Petroleum 

Authority for the year 2024 was submitted pursuant to the Public Financial 

Management Act, 2016 (Act 921), the Public Financial Management 

Regulations, 2019 (L.I. 2378), the Revised Guidelines for the Effective 

Functioning of Audit Committees, and directives issued by the Internal 

Audit Agency. 

The Statement provided an account of the Audit Committee's oversight 

activities, including the review of internal and external audit findings, the 

implementation of audit recommendations, enterprise risk management, 

and the strengthening of internal control and corporate governance 

systems. - 

3.0 REFERENCE DOCUMENTS 

The Committee referred to and was guided by the following documents 

during its deliberations on the Statement: 

i.  The 1992 Constitution of the Republic of Ghana; 

i, The Standing Orders of the Parliament of Ghana; 

iii.  National Petroleum Authority Act, 2005 (Act 691) 

iv.  The Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921); 

v. The Public Financial Management Regulations, 2019 (L.I. 2378); 

vi.  The Audit Committee Guidelines (2023). 

4.0 SCOPE OF THE STATEMENT 

The Statement examined the following:

5.0 

5.1 

« Effectiveness of internal controls and compliance with financial 

regulations. ) 

e Status of implementation of all audit recommendations issued in 

2024. 

« Integrity of revenue collection, receivables management and banking 

arrangements. 

+ Adequacy of technical operations. 

+ Governance arrangements suppoerting risk management and audit 

oversight. 

OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 

The Audit Committee reviewed all the audit findings and recommendations 

in respect of the Authority for the year under review. The Committee noted 

that most audit issues had been successfully resolved by the Authority. 

However, the following issues were not fully resolved: 

Inventory and Stores Management Weaknesses 

The Statement observed that the National Petroleum Authority (NPA) had 

significant weaknesses in [ts stores management system at one of its 

regional offices, including the absence of shelves, the failure to assign a 

dedicated stores officer, inadequate stores documentation and poor 

inventory management practices. 

The Committee noted that although management had acknowledged the 

deficiencies, the corrective measures had remained outstanding beyond the 

implementation timeline, with the Authority attributing the delay to 

budgetary constraints and a decision to seek approval to expand the 

corrective interventions to cover all regional offices. 

The Committee recommends that management expedites the completion 

of the stores improvement programme across all regional offices and 

ensure that each office is equipped with adequate storage facilities, assign 

5.2 

53 

qualified stores personnel and operate with the requisite inventory control 

documentation to strengthen accountability over public assets. 

Weak Management Oversight over Budget Performance 

The Statement observed that management did not regularly review budget 

performance reports before their submission to the Board, contrary to 

sound financial management practices. 

Although management indicated that corrective measures had since been 

introduced, the Committee considered the omission to be a fundamental 

weakness which could impinge sound corporate governance and 

accountability. 

The Committee recommends that management institutionalises periodic 

budget performance reviews at management level and ensures that all 

Heads of Department have timely access to budget performance 

information and feedback to facilitate effective financial oversight and 

decision-making. 

Outstanding Receivables and Debt Recovery Challenges 

The Audit Committee observed that the Authority continued to carry 

substantial outstanding receivables from Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs), 

including long-outstanding debts with no movement over several years. 

The Committee noted that, in response to this issue, management had 

established a Receivables Committee, and had successfully recovered 

significant amounts of outstanding debts (GHS 170,837,250.06 

successfully recovered out of a‘ total of GHS 231,729,203.95), 

deactivated defaulting entities from the electronic licensing platform and 

referred certain cases for investigation. 

The Committee recommends that management intensifies debt recovery 

efforts by strengthening the work of the Receivables- Committee, 

4 

continuously monitoring aged receivables, pursuing legal recovery actions 

where necessary and providing periodic reports on . debt recovery 

performance to help guide credit risk decisions. 

5.4 Need to Strengthen Enforcement of the Regulatory Framework 

6.0 

The Statement observed that management had identified limitations in the 

existing legislative framework as part of the key challenges affecting 

effective regulation of the downstream petroleum sector. 

The Committee was informed of the intention of management to review the 

enabling legisiation to introduce stronger enforcement and sanctioning 

powers, 

The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Energy and the National 

Petroleum Authority expedite the review of the National Petroleum 

Authority Act, 2005 (Act 691) and related regulations to strengthen 

enforcement mechanisms and enhance regulatory compliance within the 

downstream petroleum industry. 

CONCLUSION 

The Committee is satisfied that the Statement has been prepared and 

presented to Parliament in accordance with the Public Financial 

Management Act, 2016 (Act 921) and the Audit Committee Guidelines 

(2023). 

The Committee recommends to the House to adopt this report on the 

Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of the National 

Petroleum Authority for the year 2024. 

Respectfully submitted. 

. BARLIANENT OF GHANA LIBRARY 
PARLIAMENT HOUSE 

GSU - ACCRA

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON ENERGY ON THE 
ANNUAL STATEMENT BY THE AUDIT COMMITTEE OF 
TEMA OIL REFINERY (TOR) FOR THE YEAR 2024 

1.0 INTRODUCTION 

The Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of Tema Oil Refinery 

(TOR) for the year 2024 was presented to Parliament on 24t October, 2025 

in accordance with Section 88 of the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 

(Act 921) 

Pursuant to article 103 of the 1992 Constitution and Order 252 of the 

Standing Orders of Parliament, the report was referred to the Committee of 

Energy for consideration and report. 

The Committee met and considered the statement with the Managing Director 

and a team of officials from the Ministry of Energy and Green Transition and 

the Tema oil Refinery. 

The Committee is grateful to the MD of TOR and the team of officials from the 

Ministry of Energy and Tema Oil Refinery for attending upon and assisting 

the Committee during the deliberations on the Annual Statement. 

2.0 BACKGROUND 

The Tema Oil Refinery is mandated to refine crude oil into finished petroleum 

products to support national energy security and contribute to the 

stabilisation of the downstream petroleum sector. TOR remains a strategic 

national installation, and its performance has direct implications for energy 

reliability, industrial activity and foreign exchange outflows. 

The Annual Statement by the Audit Committee of TOR for 2024 was submitted 

pursuant to the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921), the Public 

Financial Management Regulations, 2019 (L.I. 2378), and the Internal Audit 

Agency Act, 2003 (Act 658). The Report provided a detailed account of internal 

audit findings, management responses and implementation status across 

1

financial management, technical operations, safety processes and governance 

systems. 

3.0 REFERENCE DOCUMENTS 

The Committee referred to and/or was guided by the following documents 

during its deliberations on the Statement:

The 1992 Constitution of the Republic of Ghana; 

The Standing Orders of Parliament; 

The Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921); 

The Public Financial Management Regulations, 2019 (L.I. 2378); 

The Audit Committee Guidelines (2023); 

4.0 OBJECTIVES AND SCOPE OF THE STATEMENT 

The Statement examined the following: 

Effectiveness of internal controls and compliance with financial 

regulations. 

Status of implementation of all audit recommendations issued in 2023 

and 2024, 

Integrity of revenue collection, receivables management and banking 

arrangements, 

Adequacy of technical operations, including maintenance of critical 

refining equipment. 

Implementation of safety protocols, hazard analyses and emergency 

preparedness. 

Governance arrangements supporting risk management and audit 

oversight. 

4.0 SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT FINDINGS 

The Audit Committee reviewed all the audit findings and recommendations in 

respect of the Refinery. The significant issues highlighted include the 

following: 

4.1 

4.2 

4.3 

Implementation of Audit Recommendations 

The Statement provided a summary of all audit recommendations requiring 

action. A total of 382 audit recommendations were recorded, out of which 56 

recommendations had been fully implemented, 213 partially implemented 

and 113 outstanding. 

The substantial number of partially implemented and unimplemented 

recommendations reflected longstanding structural limitations, inadequate 

monitoring frameworks and delayed managerial responses to audit findings. 

These outstanding recommendations spanned diverse areas including 

documentation gaps, safety compliance, financial reconciliations, 

procurement processes and asset integrity inspections. 

The Committee views compliance with audit recommendations as 

foundational to sound public financial management and emphasises the need 

for TOR to prioritise the clearance of these items. The Committee underscores 

that the continuous accumulation of unresolved audit issues undermines 

operational discipline and limits the efficiency of regulatory oversight. 

Technical and Operational Challenges 

The Audit Committee examined the deficiencies in technical operations as 

highlighted in the audit reports. The Committee observed that several critical 

equipment and utilities, such as Boiler 8, the 6.5 MW generator, and key 

compressors, remained faulty, thereby limiting the capacity of the Refinery to 

operate efficiently. 

The absence of adequate maintenance planning has contributed to persistent 

equipment failures. 

The Committee urges Management to accelerate maintenance works and 

adopt structured asset rehabilitation programmes, given the strategic 

importance of these units to the Refinery’s operations. 

Internal Control and Financial Management Issues 

3 

4.4 

4.5 

The Audit Committee examined audit observations relating to internal 

controls and noted material weaknesses in receivables management, bank 

reconciliation, treasury operations and revenue assurance practices. 

The Statement observed the presence of dormant accounts, delayed 

transaction postings, incomplete reconciliations and unexplained variances 

between Treasury records and operational accounts. These gaps undermined 

financial integrity and operational predictability. 

The Committee underscored that maintaining accurate financial records is 

essential to transparency, efficient cash-flow planning and compliance with 

the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921). 

The Committee advises TOR to strengthen its internal audit function, enforce 

reconciliation schedules, enhance documentation quality and introduce 

modern financial management systems to support accuracy and 

accountability. 

Governance and Oversight Arrangements 

The Audit Committee reviewed matters relating to governance and noted that 

the inauguration of a new Audit Committee in April 2024 had improved the 

oversight environment. However, the execution of audit directives still require 

greater urgency due to non-operationalisation of the Refinery during the 

period under reference. 

The Committee observed that the persistence of unresolved audit issues 

across multiple years reflected weaknesses in internal governance 

mechanisms and called for more assertive enforcement of directives and 

better alignment between Management and the Audit Committee. 

The Committee emphasises the need for effective governance through regular 

follow-up actions, timely managerial responses and consistent documentation 

of progress. 

‘Strategic Position and Capital Requirements of TOR 
4 

5.0 

5.1 

5.2 

The Statement observed that TOR continues to hold a strategic position as a 

natjonal refinery with potential to contribute significantly to energy security 

and reduction of import dependency. However, the Committee noted severe 

capital iimitations affecting the ability of the Refinery to rehabilitate key 

processing units, modernise systems and secure crude oil for full operations. 

Management informed the Committee that the financial position of the 

Refinery had constrained its ability to secure letters of credit, thereby 

necessitating a shift to a tolling model where private entities supply crude for 

refining. The Committee noted that although the tolling model provides a 

temporary operational pathway, it does not address the long-term capital 

deficit. 

The Committee recommends a major capital injection to restore full refining 

capacity, upgrade aged systems and strengthen refinery resilience. 

OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 

Outstanding Audit Recommendations 

The Committee observed that although the Tema Oil Refinery had made 

progress in addressing certain audit infractions, substantial operational, 

financial and technical challenges continued to impede the full 

implementation of audit recommendations. 

The Committee therefore recommends that Management prioritise the 

clearance of all outstanding audit recommendations, particularly those 

relating to technical operations, safety compliance and financial 

management so as to improve operational efficiency and strengthen 

accountability. 

Financial Constraints and Operational Restoration 

The Committee noted that financial constraints had adversely affected 

maintenance activities, safety systems and the execution of critical capital 

projects necessary for the operational restoration of the Refinery. 

5 l PARLIAMENT OF GHANA LIBRARY 
PARLIAMENT HOUSE 

OSU - ACCRA 

5.3 

54 

6.0 

The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Energy collaborates closely 

with the Refinery and the Ministry of Finance to mobilise and secure 

adequate funding to support essential rehabilitation works, maintenance 

programmes and operational upgrades. 

Internal Controls, Safety Compliance and Governance 

The Committee observed that weaknesses in internal control systems, delays 

in safety compliance and inadequate engagement between Management and 

the Audit Committee continued to affect operational efficiency and 

institutional confidence. 

The Committee therefore recommends the strengthening of internal control 

mechanisms, the prompt enforcement of safety protocols and enhanced 

coordination between Management and the Audit Committee to ensure the 

timely implementation of directives and audit recommendations. 

Management Efforts despite Operational Challenges 

The Committee commended the Management of the Tema Oil Refinery for the 

efforts made to sustain Refinery despite the significant operational challenges 

and debt burden confronting the entity. The Committee encouraged 

Management to continue pursuing measures aimed at improving operational 

performance, financial sustainability and institutional resilience. 

CONCLUSION 

The Committee is satisfied that the Statement has been prepared and 

presented to Parliament in accordance with the Public Financial Management 

Act, 2016 (Act 921) and the Audit Committee Guidelines (2023). 

The Committee recommends to the House to adopt this report on the Annual 

Statement by the Audit Committee of Tema Oil Refinery for the year 2024. 

Respectfully submitted.

ON THE

REPORT OF THE FINANCE COMMITTEE ON THE CONTRACT 

AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOYERNMENT OF THE, REPUBLIC 
OF GHANA (REPRESENTED BY THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE) AND i
