IN RESPECT OF THE RENEWAL OF HEADLEASE FOR REGINA 

HOUSE, LONDON, UNITED KINGDOM, WHICH PROVIDES 
ACCOMMODATION FOR GHANA INTERNATIONAL BANIK (GHIB) 

1.0 INTRODUCTION 

The Contract Agreement between the Government of the Republic of' Ghana (represented 

by the Ministry of Finance) and Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Mercers in 

respect of the Renewal of Headlease for Regina House London, United Kingdom, which 

provides accommodation for Ghana [nternational Bank (GHIB) was presented to the 

House on Wednesday, 24" June, 2026, by the Hon Minister for Finance in accordance 

with Article 181(5) of the Constitution. 

The Agreement was subsequently referred to the Finance Committee for consideration 
and report in accordance with the Standing Orders of the Parliament of Ghana. 

2.0 DELIBERATIONS 

The Committee met with the Hon Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Baah Forson; the 

Hon Deputy Minister for Finance, Mr Thomas Nyarko Ampem; and the technical team 

from the Ministry of Finance to discuss the Referral. 

The Committee is grateful to the Hon Deputy Minister and the officials for attending 

upon the Committee. 

3.0 REFERENCE DOCUMENTS 

The Committee referred to the following documents during the deliberations: 

i The Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992; 

i The Standing Orders of Parliament, 2024; 

ili Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921); 

iv. The Headlease for Regina House, London, United Kingdom; 

v The Draft Deed of Lease Extension: 

vi The Property Valuation Report for Regina House, London, United Kingdom; 

vii  Legal Opinion on the Renewal of the Headlease; 

viii - Financial and Technical Assessment Report in refation to the Headlease; and 

ix  Parliamentary Memorandum submitted by the Hon Minister for Finance, Dr 

Cassiel Ato Baah Forson, dated 1™ June, 2026. 

Pagelof3

4.0 

5.0 

6.0 

6.1 

6.2 

6.3 

BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE PROPERTY 

Regina House is a London property occupied by Ghana International Bank. 

The current Headlease was granted by the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of 

Mercers of the City of London to the Government of Ghana, acting through the President, 

which commenced in September 1937 and expires in September 2027. 

In 2022, the Mercers (the Headlessors) indicated their willingness to negotiate further 

terms with the Government of Ghana. On 5" March, 2026, GHIB, through Capital Real 

Estate Partners as informal commeicial real-estate advisers, submitted an offer for the 

lease extension. The Mercers then formally approved the Government’s offer on 200 

March 2026. 

DURATION OF THE PROPOSED HEADLEASE 

The duration of the proposed headlease is one hundred and fifty (150) years. 

OBSERVATIONS 

The Committee made the following observations during the deliberations: 

Renewal of Headlease 

The Committee observed that the Agreement makes a strategic case for renewing the 

Headlease. Renewal of the lease ties the property to Ghana’s financial representation n 

the UK, the operational continuity of GHIB, service delivery to the Ghanaian diaspora, 

and the preservation of a strategically located and historically significant state asset. It 

also emphasises the risk of disruption, increased costs, and reputational damage if 

renewal is delayed or fails. These are material public-interest considerations, especiaily 

given the stated September 2027 expiry date and the lead time typically required for UK 

property transactions. 

The Committee also observed that the proposed consideration of £17.25 million is 

described as negotiated and accepted by the Mercers. 

Appointment of UK-Based Legal and Commercial Advisers 

The Committee uoted that the exact purchasing entity must still be confirmed, that UK~ 

based legal and commercial advisers must be appointed urgently to review title and Land 

Registry and that unilateral notices connected with a dispute involving GPGC Limited 

must be removed. 

Cost of property 

The Committee further noted that securing the leasehold will require an initial investment 

of at least £17.25 million, but a separate preliminary estimate suggests an overall outlay 

of £22 million to £25 million once the lease premium, refurbishment, and professional 
fees are included. The Committee identified refurbishment costs of £1.5 million to £2 
million, a commercial adviser fee of £140,000 exclusive of VAT, an abortive fee cap of 

£25,000 exclusive of VAT, legal adviser fees estimated at £60,000 to £80,000 excluding 

VAT or other sales tax, and additional Land Registry and banking fees. 

Page 20f3

6.4 Rental Income 

The Comumittee also observed that current annual rental income could exceed £1,394,94 1 

and that, on stated assumptions, the investment would recover its initial cost in 

approximately 12.4 years. 

6.5 Recommended Option for Headlease 

The Committee observed that there are two options. One is the renewal of the Headlease 

and maintain Regina House, or decline renewal and relocate GHIB. On the evidence 

presented, the first option is understandably preferred. The Committee has carefully 

considered the Agreement and is of the view that when ratified, the Headlease for Regina 

House will be in the best interest of the Republic of Ghana. 

In summary, the Commitiee noted that Regina House remains a strategic national asset 

that supports Ghana’s diplomatic presence in the United Kingdom. The expiry of the 

existing Headlease makes the renewal both necessary and urgent. Professional valuation, 

legal and technical assessments have also been undertaken to support the proposed 

renewal. The Committee also noted that the proposed renewal is more economical than 

acquiring a comparable property in the same locality and renewal of the Headlease would 

preserve Ghana’s long-term investment and avoid the substantial costs and operational 

disruptions associated with relocation. 

7.0 CONCLUSION 

The Committee concluded that the Contract Agreement makes a credible strategic case 

for renewal of the Regina House Headlease. The proposed renewal appears aligned with 

the Government’s stated policy objectives of preserving a strategic overseas asset, 

sustaining GHIB's role, and retaining a foothold in a major international financial centre. 

The Committee, therefore, recommends to the House to adopt this report and ratify the 

Contract Agreement between the Government of the Republic of Ghana (represented by 

the Ministry of Finance) and Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Mercers in 

respect of the Renewal of Headlease for Regina House London, United Kingdom, which 

provides accommodation for Ghana International Bank (GHIB) in accordance with 

Atticle 181 (5) of the 1992 Constitution and the Standing Orders of the House. 

Respectfully submitted

text:
IN THE SECOND MEETING OF THE SECOND SESSION 

OF THE NINTH PARLIAMENT OF THE 

FOURTH REPUBLIC OF GHANA | 

REPORT OF THE FINANCE COMMITTEE 

ON THE 

BASIC DOCUMENTS OF THE EUROPEAN BANK FOR 

RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT (EBRD) TO FACILITATE 

GHANA’S SUBSCRIPTION TO FIVE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-TWO 

(522) SHARES OF THE CAPITAL STOCK OF THE EBRD 

MAY 2026

REPORT OF THE FINANCE COMMITTEE ON THE 

BASIC DOCUMENTS OF THE EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND 

DEVELOPMENT (EBRD) TO FACILYTATE GHANA’S SUBSCRIPTION TO FIVE 

HUNDRED AND TWENTY-TWO (522) SHARES OF THE CAPITAL STOCK OF 

THE EBRD 

1.0 INTRODUCTION 

On Wednesday, 25% March, 2026, the Hon Deputy Minister for Finance, Mr Thomas 

Nyarko Ampem laid in Parliament the Basic Documents of the European Bank for 

Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) to facilitate Ghana’s subseription to five 

hundred and twenty-two (522) shares of the capital stock of the EBRD in accordance 

with Article 75(2) of the 1992 Constitution. 

The Speaker subsequently referred the Basic Documents of the EBRD to the Finance 

Committee for consideration and report in accordance with the Standing Orders of 

Parliament. 

2.0 DELIBERATIONS 

‘The Committee met with Officials of the Ministry to consider the referral. 

‘The Committee is grateful to the Officials for attending upon the Committee and assisting 
in the deliberations. 

3.0 REFERENCE DOCUMENTS 

The Committee referred to the following documents during the deliberations: 

i The Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992; 

ii.  The Standing Orders of Parliament, 2024; 

iii. Exccutive Approval for Ghana's Accession to the European Bank for 

Reconstruction and Development; and 

iv.  Memorandum to Parliament by the Minister for Finance on Ghana’s Accession to 

the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). 

4.0 BACKGROUND INFORMATION 

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development was established in 1991 with 

the primary objective of fostering the transition to open, market-oriented economies and 

promoting private sector development. Over the years, the Bank has evolved into a major 

multilateral development finance institution supporting infrastructure development, 

financial sector deepening, and sustainable economic growth.

5.0 

6.0 

6.1 

Although the EBREs initial focus was on Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia, 

its operations have progressively expanded to other regions, including selected countries 

in Africa. This expansion reflects the Bank’s commitment to supporting emerging and 

developing cconomies in addressing infrastructure deficits, enhancing private sector 

competitiveness, and strengthening economic resilience. 

Ghana’s decision to accede to the EBRD forms part of a broader national strategy to 

diversify sources of development financing and reduce overreliance on traditional 

multilateral and bilateral partners. The accession is also intended to position Ghana to 

benefit from the Bank’s financing instruments, technical expettise, and policy advisory 

services. 

It is therefore imperative to subject the Basic Documents for Parliamentary approval in 

accordance with Article 75(2) of the 1992 Constitution. 

EXECUTIVE APPROVAL 

His Excellency the President of the Republic has granted Executive Approval for the 

ratification of the Treaty, in accordance with established constitutional practice. This 

approval signifies the Executive’s commitment to Ghana’s accession and paves the way 

for Parliamentary consideration and approval of the Agreement. 

EBRD’s operational model places strong emphasis on private sector-led growth, with a 

significant proportion of its investments directed toward private enterprises. This aligns 

with Ghana’s development agenda, which prioritises industrialisation, entrepreneurship, 

and job creation. 

Additionally, membership of the EBRD will enable Ghana to participate in the 

governance of the Bank, including decision-making processes relating to investments 

and policy direction, thereby enhancing Ghana’s voice in international financial affairs. 

BASIC DOCUMENTS OF THE EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION 

AND DEVELOPMENT (EBRD) 

The Basic Documents contain the Agreement establishing the European Bank for 

Reconstruction and Development, the Chaitman’s Report on the Agreement and the By- 

Laws of EBRD. The Documents outline the following: 

Purpose, Functions and Membership 

This chapter establishes the Bank’s purpose which is to promote transition towards open 

market-oriented  economies, private enterprise and entrepreneurship in countries 

commitied to multiparty democracy, pluralism and market economics. It also provides 

for the Bank’s operations in Mongolia, Southern and Eastern Medilerranean countries, 

and a limited number of sub-Saharan African member countries. The chapter further 

outlines the Bank’s functions, including support for private-sector development, capital

that fails to fulfil its obligations. A suspended member loses rights except the right of 

withdrawal but remains subject to obligations. The Chapter further provides for 

settlement of accounts with former members and procedures for temporary suspension 

or termination of the Banlc’s operations. 

Status, Immunities, Privileges and Exemptions 

This chapter gives the Bank legal personality and capacity to contract, own and dispose 

of property, and institute legal proceedings. It provides immunities for the Bank’s assets, 

archives and official communications, and sets out privileges and immunities for 

Governors, Directors, officers, employees and experts. It also covers tax exemptions and 

states that immunities are granted in the Bank’s interest and may be waived where 

appropriate. 

Amendments, Interpretation and Arbitration 

This chapter sets out how the Agreement may be amended, including voting thresholds 

and matters requiring unanimous acceplance. [t also provides that interpretation 

questions are first submitted to the Board of Directors, with appeal to the Board of 

Governors. Disputes involving the Bank and a former member, or disputes after 

termination of operations arc to be submitted to arbitration by a three-member tribunal 

whose decision is final and binding. 

Tinal Provisions 

This chapter covers signature, deposit, ratification, acceptance or approval of the 

Agreement, entry into force, the inaugural meeting and commencement of operations. It 

states that the Agreement was done at Paris on 29" May, 1990, in English, French, 

German and Russian, all texts being equally authentic. 

Letter from the Chairman of the Conference 

The letter records the understanding reached by members to follow the normal practice 

of using the Bank’s working languages according to its day to day needs and taking into 

consideration the interests of efficiency and economy. 

By-Laws of EBRD 

The By-Laws are complementary to the Agreement establishing EBRD which spell out 

the location of the Principal Office of the Bank and branches. It also spells out rules of 

procedure for Board of Governors, conditions of service of Governors, Directors, 

President and Vice President(s). The By-Laws also contain the Code of Conduct 

concerning inter alia personal investment holdings and transactions, Delegation of 

Powers by Board of Directors and special representation of members at meetings of the 

Board of Directors.

mobilisation, infrastructure, technical assistance, capital markets, regional projects and 

sustainable development. Membership is open to European countries, non-European IMF 

members, the Buropecan Community and the European Investment Bank. 

Capifal 

This chapter deals with the Bank’s authorised capital, subscription of shares, payment of 

subscriptions, and ordinary capital resources. The original authorised capital stock is 

divided into shares, with subscriptions made by members. It distinguishes between paid- 

in shares and callable shares, sets rules for capital increases and confirms that no member 

is obliged to subscribe to future capital increases. It also limits members” liability to the 

unpaid portion of their shares and siates that members are not liable for the Bank’s 

obligations merely by being members. 

Borrowing and Other Miscellaneous Powers 

The chapter gives the Bank general powers to borrow funds, invest or deposit funds not 

immediately needed, buy and sell securities, guarantee securities, underwrite securities, 

provide technical advice, make rules necessary for its functions and enter cooperation 

agroements with public or private entities. It also states that securities issued or 

guaranteed by the Bank are not obligations of any govermment or member unless 

expressly stated. 

Currencies 

This chapter provides rules on currency determination and use. The Bank determines 

whether a currency is fully convertible, taking account of its financial interests and 

consulting the IMF where necessary. Members are prohibited from imposing restrictions 

on the Bank’s receipt, holding, use or transfer of currencies received through capital 

subscriptions, borrowings, Special Funds or repayments from Bank operations. 

Organisation and Management 

This chapter establishes the Bank’s governance structure which includes; Board of 

Governors, Board of Direclors, President, Vice-Presidents, officers and staff. It defines 

the composition and powers of the Board of Governors, including admission ol members, 

capital changes, suspension of members, election of Directors and the President, approval 

of accounts, amendment of the Agreement and termination of operations. [t also covers 

the Board of Directors, voting, the President’s role, staff recruitment, the Bank’s 

international character, office location, depositories, reporting duties and distribution of 

net income. 

‘Withdrawal, Suspension and Termination of Operations 

This chapter provides that a member may withdraw by written notice, with withdrawal 

taking effect not less than six months after notice. 1t also allows suspension of a member

The By-Laws also provide for vacant directorships, report of the Board of Directors, 

when the financial year begins and ends, audits and budget, application for membership 

of the Bank, suspension of a member and a provision for amendments to the By-Laws, 

OBSERVATIONS 

‘The Committee made the following observations during the deliberations: 

Strategic Importance 

The Committee noted that Ghana’s accession (o the European Bank for Reconstruction 

and Development (EBRD) is in line with its policy objective of diversifying sources of 

development finance and strengthening international economic cooperation. 

The Committee also noted that Ghana’s accession to EBRD will enable the country 

access affordable long-term financing for key sectors of the economy, including 

agribusiness, energy, financial institutions, manufacturing, infrastructure, property, 

tourism, telecommunications, and media thereby complementing existing funding 

S0urces. 

The Committee observed that Ghana’s accession will also reduce the burden of 

government guarantees for state-funded projects where the EBRD could provide 

guarantees. Ghana’s membership would strengthen regional integration and cooperation 

with member countries in Europe, Central Asia, and the Southern and Eastern 

Mediterrancan. 

Promotion of Private Sector Development 

The Committee observed that the EBRD’s emphasis on private sector-led growth 

presents significant opportunities for Ghanaian businesses, particularly smail and 

medium-sized enterprises, to expand and become more competitive. 

The Committee noted that future loans to public entities, SOEs, or private-sector 

participants would be subject to separate eredit, risk, and guarantee assessments, and that 

any sovereign guarantee requirements would come back through the appropriate 

parliamentary process, 

Arbitration 

On legal recourse, the Committee noted that disputes would largely be handled through 

the bank’s agreed dispute mechanisms, including arbitration, and that Ghanaian courts 

would not necessarily have unrestricted jurisdiction over all matters involving the bank 

especially if the regional headquarters of the Bank is situated in Ghana. 

7.4 Financial implications 

The Committee noted that Ghana’s financial commitment under the Agreement consists 

of both paid-in and callable capital. While the paid-in capital constitutes a direct financial 

obligation, the callable capital represents a contingent fiability that is not expected to 

crystallise under normal circumstances. 

The Officials from the Ministry of Finance informed the Committee that Ghana’s 

accession would involve a paid-in subscription of €950,000, derived from the paid-in 

portion of Ghana’s proposed sharcholding. 

7.5 Technical and Institational Support 

The Committes further observed that the EBRD provides technical assistance and policy 

advisory services, which will contribute to strengthening Ghana’s institutional capacity, 

improving regulatory frameworks, and enhancing governance. 

8.0 CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATION 

The Commitiee, having thoroughly examined the Agreement on Ghana’s accession 
to 

the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, is of the considered 
view that 

the accession will enhance Ghana’s access to development financing, promote private 

sector growth, and support the country’s economic transformation agenda. 

The Committee is satisfied that the legal requirements for the approval of the Agreement 

have been duly complied with and that the financial obligations arising from the 

accession are sustainable. 

The Commitiee urges Government to ensure effective coordination, monitoring, 
and 

reporting in respect of all engagements with the EBRD to maximise the benefits of 

membership while safeguarding the national interest. 

The Commitiee further recommends to the House to adopt this Report and ratify the 

Agreement on the Accession of the Republic of Ghana to the European Bank for 

Reconstruction and Development in accordance with Article 75(2) of the 1992 

Constitution. 

Respectfully submitted.

text:
IN THE SECOND SESSION OF THE NINTH PARLIAMENT OF 

THE FOURTH EPUBLIC OF GHANA 

REPORT NO: LEG/9/2/2/003 

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL 

AND LEGAL AFFAIRS 

ON THE 

CONDUCT OF PUBLIC OFFICERS BILL, 2026 

JULY, 2026

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEFE, ON CONSTITUTIONAL AND LEGAL 

AFFAJIRS ON THE ON THE CONDUCT OF PUBLIC OFFICERS BILL, 

2026 

1.0 INTRODUCTION 

The Conduct of Public Officers Bill, 2026 was laid in Parliament by Hon. 

Emmanuel Armah Kofi Buah, Member of Parliament for Ellembele on behalf of 

the Attorney-General and Minister for Justice, Hon. Dr. Dominic Akuritinga 

Ayine, in accordance with Order 163 of the Standing Orders of the Parliament 

and read the first time on Friday, 26 June 2026. 

Rt Hon Speaker subsequently referred the Bill to the Committee on Constitutional 

and Legal Affairs for consideration and report, in accordance with article 106(4) 

of the 1992 Constitution and Order 238 of the Standing Orders of Parliament. 

The Committee met with the Attorney General and Minister for Justice, Hon. Dr. 

Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, Madam Fati Bodua Seidu, Chief Director of the 

Office of the Attorney-General and Ministry of Justice; and officials of the Office 

of the Attorney-General and Ministry of Justice. 

The Committee is grateful to all individuals who assisted in its consideration of 

the Bill. 

2.0 REFERENCE DOCUMENTS 

The Committee referred to the following documents in its consideration of the 

Bill: 

i. The 1992 Constitution of Ghana; 

ii. The Public Officers Act, 1962 (Act 114); 

1| Pag-

iii. The Public Office Holder's (Declaration of Assets and Disqualification) 

Act, 1998 (Act 550); 

iv. The Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice Act, 1993 

(Act 456); 

v. The Public Financial Management Act, 2016 {Act 921); 

vi. The Public Procurement Act, 2003 (Act 663); 

vii. The Internal Audit Agency Act, 2003 (Act 658); 

viil. The Audit Service Act, 2000 (Act 584); 

ix. The Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2020 (Act 1044); 

x. The Economic and Organised Crime Office Act, 2010 (Act 804); 

xi. The Narcotics Control Commission Act, 2020 (Act 1019); 

xii. The United Nations Convention against Corruption, ratified by 

Parliament on 16th December, 2005; 

xiii. The African Union Convention on Preventing and Combating Corruption, 

ratified by Parliament on 13th June, 2007; 

xiv.The Oaths Act, 1972 (INR.C.D. 6); and 

xv. The Conduct of Public Officers Bill, 2026. 

4.0 OBJECT OF THE BILL 

The object of the Bill is to give effect to Chapter 24 of the 1992 Constitution by 

providing for the conduct of public officers in the performance of their functions, 

and to domesticate the United Nations Convention against Corruption and the 

African Union Convention on Preventing and Combating Corruption. 

4.1 Contents of the Bill 

The Bill has Fifty-Seven (57) clauses and three (3) Schedules. 

2{rage

Clause 1 provides for the qualifications for holding public office. Clause 2 

provides for the effective date of an adverse finding, while Clause 3 specifies the 

circumstances under which a public officer may continue to hold office. 

Clause 4 provides for the declaration of assets and Clause 5 is on labilities and 

the categories of assets required to be declared. Clauses 6 and 7 deal with assets 

acquired after the submission of a declaration and the accuracy of information 

contained in a declaration. 

Clauses 8 is on requests for clarification. Clause 9 provides for the consequences 

of a public officer's failure to submit a declaration or provide the required 

clarification. 

Clause 10 deals with declarations made under the Act is admissible in evidence 

before a court. 

Clauses 11 and 12 provide for complaints relating to contraventions of the Act 

and the confidentiality of information obtained under the Act. 

Clauses 13 covers publication and retention of declarations. Clause 14 provides 

for retention of information by the Auditor-General. 

Clauses 15 provides for the Code of Conduct. Clause 16 deals with publication 

of the code of conduct in the Gazette and on the website of the Public Services 

Commission. 

Clause 17 is on the performance of official functions, while Clause 18 prohibits 

the use of public office for personal gain or for the benefit of another person. 

Clause 19 algo prohibits sexual harassment by a public officer, while Clause 20 

bans the solicitation or acceptance of gifts, advantages or favours. 

3fPage 

i 
i { 

Clauses 21 and 22 provide for acceptable gifts and impose a duty on public 

officers to account for gifts received. 

Clause 23 provides for the avoidance of conflicts of interest. Clause 24 imposes 

a duty to report conflicts of interest. 

Clauses 25 and 26 regulate business interests and the award of contracts. Clause 

27 deals with financial interests. 

Clause 28 prohibits a public officer from using his or her office for personal 

benefit. Clauses 29 and 30 regulate the sale or gifting of Government assets by 

public officers and impose a duty to protect and preserve public property. 

Clause 31 requires public officers to maintain political neutrality in the discharge 

of their official duties. 

Clause 32 is on Political neutrality and Clause 33 require public officers to 

provide official advice and information honestly, impartially, and without fear or 

favour, and prohibit the provision of false or misleading information in the 

performance of official functions. 

Clause 34 regulates the conduct of the private affairs of public officers, while 

Clause 35 provides for the selection of public officers. 

Clause 36 prohibits a public officer from causing another person to perform an 

act which, if performed by the public officer, would constitute a contravention of 

the Act. 

Clause 37 provides for the reporting of improper directives, while Clause 38 

prohibits the consumption of alcoholic beverages or psychotropic substances 

while performing the functions of that officer. 

4 Page

Clauses 39 and 40 provide for the vindication of the conduct of a public officer 

and publication in the media. Clause 41 regulates the communication of official 

information. 

Clauses 42 to 44 are on investigations and actions to be taken following 

investigations by the Commissioner. 

Clauses 45 and 46 provide for referrals for criminal proceedings and the 

publication of actions taken. Clauses 47 and 48 prescribes directives to public 

officers and the general sanctions for contraventions of the Act. 

Clauses 49 and 50 make provision for oaths to be taken by public officers and the 

signing of the Code of Conduct. 

Clause 51 is on post-employment restrictions, while Clause 52 requires the Fair 

Wages and Salaries Commission to provide information relating to the salaries of 

public officers. 

Clause 53 provides for the duty of public officers to cooperate with the Attorney- 

General. Clauses 54 and 55 provide for the making of Regulations and the 

interpretation of the Act. 

Finally, Clauses 56 and 57 provide for repeals, savings, and transitional 

provisions. 

5.0 OBSERVATIONS 

5.1 Rationale for the Bill 

The Committee observed that the object of the Bill is to provide a legal framework 

to regulate the conduct of public officers in the performance of their official 

functions and to govern the declaration of assets by public officers. 

5]rage 

The Attorney-General indicated that the Bill was necessary to address an existing 

legislative gap and to give full effect to Chapter Twenty-Four of the Constitution 

by establishing a comprehensive legal framework to regulate the conduct of 

public officers, manage conflicts of interest and unethical conduct, strengthen the 

asset declaration regime, and provide effective mechanisms for investigation, 

enforcement, and sanctions. 

The Attorney-General further stated that, although the Commission on Human 

Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ) has issued Guidelines on Conflict of 

Interest since 2006, those Guidelines do not have the force of law and are 

therefore not legally enforceable. 

Additionally, while various enactments contain provisions relating to codes of 

conduct and conflicts of interest, these provisions are fragmented across several 

laws and do not adequately deter corruption, conflicts of interest, unexplained 

wealth, or other forms of uncthical conduct. 

The Attorney-General informed the Committee that the Bill secks (o address these 

gaps by strengthening the legal framework governing the conduct of public 

officers, including provisions for lifestyle audits, thereby enhancing integrity, 

accountability, and transparency in public administration. He further noted that 

the Bill is intended to fulfil Ghana's international obligations relating to anti- 

corruption and good governance and to improve the country’s performance on the 

Corruption Perceptions Index. 

The Bill also seeks to domesticate Ghana's obligations under the United Nations 

Convention against Corruption and the African Union Convention on Preventing 

and Combating Corruption, both of which were ratified by Parliament on 16 

December 2005 and 13 June 2007, respectively. 

6| Page

The Attorney-General emphasized that every public officer occupies a position 

of trust and is expected to serve the best interests of the public. He stated that 

achieving zero tolerance for corruption, particularly unethical conduct and 

practices among public officers, requires the effective implementation of 

legislation that establishes and enforces clear standards of ethics, transparency, 

accountability, and integrity in governance. 

The Attorney-General concluded that the Bill is necessary because it provides an 

effective deterrent against unethical conduct, strengthens accountability in public 

administration, promotes ethical behaviour among public officers, and helps 

restore public confidence in public institutions. 

5.2 Establishment of the Public Ethics Commission 

The Committee was informed that, to ensure the effective implementation and 

enforcement of the provisions of the Act, it was necessary to establish a body to 

oversee its administration and enforcement. 

The Attorney-General informed the Committee that the Government proposes the 

establishment of a Public Ethics Commission as a statutory body responsible for 

administering and enforcing the Act. 

The proposed Commission will receive and determine complaints, investigate 

alleged misconduct and unethical conduct by public officers, and verify 

declarations of assets, liabilities, and interests. In addition, the Commission will 

conduct integrity assessments, ethics compliance reviews, lifestyle audits, and 

unexplained wealth assessments. 

The Attorney-General further stated that, while the Commission will be 

responsible for the administration and enforcement of the Act, the Office of the 

7lPage

Attorney-General will retain its constitutional mandate to prosecute offences 

arising under the Act, 

5.3 Declaration and Publication of Assets 

The Committee noted that the Bill gives effect to Chapter Twenty-Four of the 

1992 Constitution by establishing a strengthened asset declaration regime. Under 

the proposed framework, public officers are required to declare their assets and 

liabilities to the Auditor-General within the prescribed timelines. In addition, the 

Bill requires the Auditor-General to publish a summary of those declarations on 

the official website of the Auditor-General. 

The Attorney-General explained that the existing asset declaration regime 

requires public office holders to declare their assets and liabilities to the Ghana 

Audit Service before assuming office, every four years while in office, and upon 

leaving office, in accordance with Article 286 of the 1992 Constitution and the 

Public Office Holders (Declaration of Assets and Disqualification) Act, 1998 

(Act 550). He noted that, under the current framework, asset declarations are kept 

in a confidential repository and are not accessible to the public. 

The Attorney-General further informed the Committee that the existing system 

has attracted considerable public criticism on the grounds that it has been 

ineffective in supporting the fight against corruption. He indicated that the current 

regime does not adequately address public concerns regarding corruption in the 

public sector, institutional weaknesses in the asset declaration system, or the 

absence of clear and uniform ethical standards governing the conduct of public 

officers. 

The Attorney-General stated that the publication of summaries of asset 

declarations under the Bill is intended to promote transparency and accountability 

by reducing the culture of secrecy surrounding the wealth of public office holders. 

8lirage 

He further explained that the publication regime is designed to enhance public 

scrutiny, encourage compliance with asset declaration obligations, deter illicit 

enrichment, and expose instances of non-compliance with the law. 

5.4 Domestication of the United Nations Convention against Corruption and 

the African Union Convention on Preventing and Combating Corruption 

The Attorney-General informed the Committee that Parliament ratified the 

United Nations Convention against Corruption on 16 December 2005. He 

explained that the Convention requires States Parties to establish systems under 

which public officials are required to declare, to the appropriate authorities, their 

assets, investments, outside employment, and substantial gifts that may give rise 

to conflicts of interest. The Convention also requires States Parties to strengthen 

domestic systems to promote transparency, prevent conflicts of interest, and 

enhance integrity in public administration. In addition, it obliges States Parties to 

adopt measures to increase transparency in public administration, including 

facilitating public access to information relating to the organisation and decision- 

making processes of public institutions, 

The Attorney-General further informed the Commitiee that Parliament ratified 

the African Union Convention on Preventing and Combating Corruption on 13 

June 2007. He explained that the Convention adopts a comprehensive approach 

to combating corruption by requiring State Parties to implement measures aimed 

at preventing, detecting, punishing, and eradicating corruption in both the public 

and private sectors. 

The Attorney-General stated that there was a need to domesticate the provisions 

of these Conventions to ensure Ghana's compliance with its international 

obligations and to strengthen the country's anti-corruption framework. He further 

indicated that the Bill seeks to give effect to these obligations by enhancing public 

9l Page

accountability, promoting integrity in public office, and strengthening 

mechanisms for preventing and combating corruption. 

5.5 Right to Privacy 

The Committee expressed concern as to whether the publication of summaries of 

asset declarations could amount to an infringement of the right to privacy of 

public officers and potentially expose them to security risks, including targeted 

attacks and kidnapping, 

The Attorney-General acknowledged the Committee's concerns but disagreed 

that the publication of summaries of asset declarations would constitute a breach 

of the constitutional right to privacy. He explained that the objective of the 

relevant provisions is to strengthen accountability among public officers by 

addressing issues relating to conflicts of interest, asset declaration, and illicit 

enrichment. 

The Attorney-General further stated that public officers occupy positions of 

public trust and are therefore subject to the constitutional standards of conduct 

prescribed under Article 284 of the Constitution. He maintained that the right to 

privacy guaranteed under Article 18 of the Constitution should not be construed 

in a manner that undermines or defeats the constitutional obligations imposed on 

public officers under Article 284, 

He further submitted that it is imperative for the State to adopt appropriate 

measures to promote transparency and accountability in the management of 

public affairs. According to the Attorney-General, the publication of summaries 

of asset declarations would enhance public confidence in the asset declaration 

regime, deter corruption and conflicts of interest, and promote greater 

accountability among public officers in the discharge of their official duties. 

0fPase 

5.6 Possible Conflict between the Bill and Codes of Conduct under Other 

Enactments 

The Attorney-General acknowledged that a number of public institutions have 

existing codes of conduct and ethical standards established under their respective 

enabling enactments or internal regulations. Ie, however, explained that the Bill 

is intended to complement those existing frameworks. 

The Attorney-General therefore indicated that, if enacted, the Bill will operate 

alongside other applicable laws, codes of conduct, and regulations governing the 

conduct of public officers, except where there is an express inconsistency 

requiting resolution in accordance with the applicable rules of statutory 

interpretation.

PUBLIC ETHICS COMMISSION 

Clause 65 — Establishment of the Public Ethics Commission 

(1) There is established by this Act a body to be known as the Public 
Ethics Commission. 

(2) The Commission is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a 
common seal and may sue and be sued in its corporate name. 

(3) The Commission shall perform its functions independently and shall 
not be subject to the direction or control of any person or authority 
except as provided by the Constitution and this Act. 

(4) The Commission is the principal statutory body responsible for 

promoting, regulating and enforcing ethical standards applicable to public 

officers under this Act. 

Clause 66 — Objects of the Commission 

The objects of the Commission are to— 

(a) promote integrity, accountability, transparency and ethical leadership 
in public administration; 

(b) secure compliance with this Act and every code of conduct applicable 
to public officers; 

14| Page 

(c) prevent corruption and unethical conduct through education, 
monitoring, compliance and enforcement measures; 

(d) strengthen institutional systems for preventing corruption, conflicts of 
interest and abuse of office; 

(&) promote public confidence in the integrity of public administration; and 

(f) complement the work of constitutional and statutory anti-corruption 

institutions through coordinated preventive and administrative measures. 

Clause 67 — Functions of the Commission 

The Commission shall— 

(a) administer and enforce this Act; 

(b) receive and determine complaints concerning alleged breaches of this 

Act; 

(¢) undertake administrative investigations into alleged misconduct or 

unethical conduct by public officers; 

(d) initiate investigations on its own motion where there are reasonable 

grounds to believe that a public officer has contravened this Act; 

(e) verify declarations of assets, liabilities and interests submitted under 

this Act; 

(f) conduct integrity assessments and ethics compliance reviews of 

Ministries, Departments, Agencies and other public institutions; 

15| Page 

(g) monitor compliance with rules relating to— 

(i) conflicts of interest; 

(ii) gifts and hospitality; 

(iii) misuse of public office; 

(iv) abuse of official information; 

(v) post-public employment restrictions; 

(vi) abuse of public resources; 

(vii) procurement ethics; and 

(viii) any other ethical obligation established under this Act; 

(h) conduet lifestyle reviews and unexplained wealth assessments for the 

purpose of determining compliance with this Act; 

(1) issue advisory opinions concerning ethical obligations under this Act; 

(§) develop codes, standards and guidelines on public ethics; 

(k) require public institutions to establish internal ethics and compliance 

systems; 

(1) provide ethics education and training for public officers; 

(m) recommend administrative, disciplinary or civil action against public 

officers; 

(n) make recommendations to the President, Parliament or any appointing 

authority for reforms necessary to improve ethical governance; 

(o) refer evidence of suspected criminal conduct to the appropriate law 

enforcement or prosecutorial authority; and 

6iPage 

(p) perform any other function conferred by this Act or any other 

enactment. 

Clause 68 — Administrative Investigative Powers 

(1) For the purpose of carrying out its functions under this Act, the 

Commission may— 

(a) receive complaints from any person; 

(b) commence investigations on its own initiative; 

(¢) require a public officer or any public institution to produce documents, 

electronic records or information relevant to an investigation; 

(d) summon persons to appear before the Commission; 

(e) examine persons on oath or affirmation; 

(f) administer oaths; 

(g) inspect records maintained by public institutions; 

(h) require written explanations from public officers; 

(i) engage auditors, forensic accountants, valuers or other experts; 

() conduct ethics audits and compliance inspections; 

(k) require a public officer to explain the source of assets or benefits where 

necessary for determining compliance with this Act; 

(1) request information from regulatory bodies or financial institutions in 

accordance with applicable law; and 

(m) apply to the High Court for such orders as may be necessary for the 

production or preservation of evidence. 

17 vage

(2) The Comimissjon shall not— 

(a) exercise powers of criminal arrest; 

(b) institute criminal prosecutions; 

(c) undertake criminal investigations reserved by law to another 

investigative authority; or 

(d) exercise powers inconsistent with the constitutional mandate of the 

Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice or any other 

constitutional body. 

(3) Nothing in this Act prevents the Commission from conducting an 

administrative investigation notwithstanding that the same facts arc the 

subject of a criminal investigation or criminal proceedings, except where 

the continuation of the administrative investigation is likely to prejudice 

those proceedings. 

Clause 69 — Findings and Administrative Orders 

Where the Commission determines that a public officer has contravened 

this Act, it may— 

(a) issue a warning or reprimand; 

(b) issue compliance directions; 

(c) direct the rectification of a conflict of interest; 

(d) order the surrender or forfeiture of prohibited gifts or benefits to the 

State; 

(¢) direct compliance with asset declaration obligations; 

18 |Page 

(f) recommend disciplinary proceedings to the appropriate disciplinary 

authority; 

(g) recommend suspension from office pending disciplinary proceedings 

where authorised by law; 

(h) recommend removal from office where authorised by the Constitution 

or another enactment; 

(i) impose administrative penaltics prescribed under this Act; 

(i) publish its findings in accordance with this Act; or 

(k) make any other administrative order authorised by this Act. 

Clause 70 — Referral of Criminal Conduct 

(1) Where, in the course of an investigation, the Commission obtains 

evidence disclosing the commission of a criminal offence, the Commission 

shall promptly refer the matter together with the evidence obtained to the 

appropriate competent authority. 

(2) A referral under subsection (1) may be made to— 

(a) the Attorney-General; 

(b) the Ghana Police Service; 

(c) the Economic and Organised Crime Office; 

(d) the Office of the Speciai Prosecutor; or 

(e) any other authority having lawful jurisdiction. 

19| Fage 

(3) The referral of a matter under this section shall not prevent the 

Commission from taking administrative measures authorised under this 

Act unless those measures are likely to prejudice the criminal investigation 

or prosecution. 

Clause 71 ~ Duty to Cooperate 

Every public institution shall cooperate with the Commission in the 

performance of its functions and shall provide such information, records 

and assistance as the Commission may reasonably require. 

Clause 72 — Relationship with Other Constitutional and Statutory 

Bodies 

(1) In performing its functions, the Commission shall cooperate with 

constitutional and statutory bodies responsible for preventing, 

investigating or prosecuting corruption and other misconduct. 

(2) The Commission shall avoid unnecessary duplication of investigations 

and may establish joint investigation or information-sharing arrangements 

with other public institutions. 

(3) Nothing in this Act shall be construed as— 

(a) limiting the constitutional functions of the Commission on Human 

Rights and Administrative Justice; 

(b) limiting the constitutional powers of the Attorney-General; 

(c) limiting the statutory functions of the Office of the Special Prosecutor; 

20| vage 

(d) fimiting the powers of the Economic and Organised Crime Office or 

any other investigative authority. 

Clause 73 — Annual State of Public Ethics Report 

The Commission shall submit to Parliament, through the President, an 

annual report containing— 

(a) an assessment of ethical compliance across the public service; ! 

(b) statistics on complaints, investigations and administrative sanctions; 

() systemic weaknesses identified, 

(d) recommendations for legislative and institutional reforms; and 

(¢) any other matter relevant to promoting integrity im public 

administration. 

7.0 CONCLUSION 

The Committee, having carefully considered the Conduct of Public Officers Bill, 

2026, is satisfied that the Bill gives meaningful effect to Chapter 24 of the 1992 

Constitution, domesticates Ghana's obligations under the United Nations 

Convention against Corruption and the African Union Convention on Preventing 

and Combating Corruption. 

The Committee unanimously recommends that this Honourable House adopts this 

Report and pass the Conduct of Public Officers Bill, 2026, in accordance with 

article 106 of the 1992 Constitution of the Republic of Ghana.

IN THE SECOND SESSION OF THE NINTIH PARLIAMENT 

OF THE FOURTH REPUBLIC OF GHANA 

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON ECONOMY AND 

DEVELOPMENT 

ON THE 

CONDUCT OF MONETARY POLICY, MACROECONOMIC 

REVIEW AND BANKING SECTOR DEVELOPMENTS 

MAY, 2026 

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON ECONOMY AND DEVELOPNMENT ON 

THE CONDUCT OF MONETARY POLICY, MACROECONOMIC REVIEW AND 

BANKING SECTOR DEVELOPMENTS, 2025 

1.0 

2.0 

3.0 

INTRODUCTION 

Pursuant to the Bank of Ghana (Amendment) Act 2016, (Act 918), 

Section 53A requires the Bank of Ghana to present half-yearly reports to 

Parliament on the conduct of activities in the exercise of its mandate at 

«the end of February and July each year. 

The Report on the Conduct of Monetary Policy, Macroeconomic Review 

and Banking Sector Development was laid in Parliament on Friday, 24 

October 2025 by the Majority Leader, Hon Mahama Ayariga. 

The report was subsequently referred by the Rt, Hon Speaker to the 

Committee on Economy and Development for consideration and report. 

DELIBERATIONS 

In considering the referral, the Committee met on Monday, 9% March 

2026, with the Governor of Bank of Ghana and officials from the Bank of 

Ghana. 

The Committée expresses its profound gratitude to the Hon. Minister and 

the officials for their attendance and assistance in the Committee's 

deliberations. 

REFERENCE DOCUMENTS 

The Committee referred to the following docurr;ents during its 

deliberations: 

i The 1992 Constitution of the Republic of Ghana; 

ii. The Standing Orders of Parliament of Ghana; 

iil.  Bank of Ghana (Amendment) Act, 2016 {Act 918); 

iv.  Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921) 

v.  Report on the Conduct of Monetary Policy, Macroeconomic 

Review and Banking Sector Developments, 2025, 

4.0 BACKGROUND 

The Committee held a statutory meeting with officials of the Bank of 

Ghana pursuant to the provisions of the amended Bank of Ghana Act 

which requires the central bank to periodically brief Parliament on 

developments in the economy and the conduct of monetary policy. The 

meeting formed part of Parliament’s oversight responsibility to ensure 

transparency and accountability in the management -of the country’s 

monetary and financial systems, 

The meeting was convened following the submission of the Bank of 

Ghana’s report on macroeconomic developments and policy actions 

undertaken during the second half of the year. 

In his introductory remarks, the Governor noted that the engagement 

with Parliament forms part of the Bank's commitment to openness and 

collaboration with the Legislature on issues relating to monetary policy, 

fi.neu;xcial stability, and the broader health of the Ghanaian economy. The 

Governor further explained that the presentation to the Committee would 

focus on four main areas, namely: the economic conditions at the 

beginning of 2025, the policy measures implemented by the Bank of 

Ghana, the macroeconomic and financial sector outcomes during the 

year, and the financial implications of those policy actions for the Bank’s 

balance sheet. 

The Governor indicated that when he assumed office in February 2025, 

the Ghanaian economy was emerging from a particularly challenging 

period characterised by sovereign debt restructuring, significant 

currency depreciation, and eclevated inflationary pressures. These 

conditions had weakened macroeconomic confidence, eroded purchasing 

power, constrained business planning, and placed pressure on the 

financial sector, Additionally, the financial system was still adjusting to 

the effects of the Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP), which 

had affected the balance sheets of financial institutions and reduced the

5.0 

income-generating capacity of Government securities held by the Bank 

of Ghana, 

Against this backdrop, the Bank of Ghana adopted a number of policy 

measures aimed at restoring macroeconomic stability, containing 

inflationary pressures, strengthening the exchange rate, and rebuilding 

confidence in the financial system. These measures included 

maintaining a tight monetary policy stance, intensifying open market 

operations to absorb excess liquidity in the banking sector, 

strengthening coordination with the Ministry of Finance, and rebuilding 

Ghana’s international reserves through improved export earnings, 

remittances, and the domestic gold purchase programme. 

The meeting therefore provided an opportunity for Members of the 

Coramittee to engage the Governor and his technical team on these 

developments, seek clarifications on policy decisions, and assess the 

implications of the Bank’s actions for macroeconomic stability and the 

broader Ghanaian economy. 

MONETARY POLICY IN GHANA 

The primary objective of the Bank of Ghana is to pursue sound monetary 

policies aimed at price stability and to create an enabling environment 

for sustainable economic growth. Price stability in this context is defined 

as a medium-term inflation target of 8 percent with a symmetric band of 

2 percent, consistent with growth at full potential, Other functions of the 

Bank of Ghana include promoting and maintaining a sound financial 

sector and payment systems through effective regulation and 

supervision. This is important because systemic risks in financial 

markets can be transmitted to the broader macroeconomy, creating 

uncertainty and undermining the objective of ensuring price stability.

6.0 OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 

The Cominittee made the following recommendations during the 

deliberation: 

6.1 Improvement in Macroeconomic Stability 

6.1.1 The Committee observed that the Bank of Ghana has made significant 

progress in restoring macroeconomic stability through a combination of 

tight monetary policy, liquidity management operations, and 

coordination with fiscal authorities. 

6.1.2 1t was noted that inflation declined sharply from 23.8 percent at the end 

of 2024 to approximately 3.3 percent in early 2026. This development 

reflects the effectiveness of the Bank’s restrictive monetary policy stance 

and its aggressive measures to absorb liquidity through open market 

operations. X 

6.1.3 While acknowledging these gains, the Committec emphasised the need 

for continued vigilance, given that macroeconomic stability remains 

yulnerable to global commodity price fluctuations and geopolitical 

developments, 

6.1.4 The Committee recommends that the Bank of Ghana continue to 

implement prudent monetary policies aimed at maintaining price 

stability and safeguarding the gains achicved in reducing inflation. 

6.2 Stabilisation and Appreciation of the Ghanaian Cedi 

5.2.1 The Committee observed that the exchange rate performance of the 

Ghanaian cedi improved considerably during the period under review. It 

was indicated that the currency appreciated significantly in 2025 

following a period of sharp depreciation in previous years. 

6.22 It was nétéd that the stabilisation of the exchange rate was supported by 

improved macroeconomic fundamentals, the rebuilding of international 

reserves, and the implementation of a new foreign exchange operational 

framework aimed at enhancing transparency in the foreign exchange 

market, 

6.2.3 The Committee also observed that improved market communication and 

the provision of forward guidance on foreign exchange inlerventions have 

4

6.2.4

6.3.2 

6.3.53 

6.3.4 

6.3.5 

reduced speculative demand for foreign currency and improved planning 

among market participants. 

The Committee recommends that the Bank of Ghana should maintain 

effective foreign exchange mariket interventions, strengthen liquidity 

management operations, and enhance its foreign reserve buffers to 

mitigate excessive volatility in the excha.ngé rate. 

Strengthening of International Reserves and Reserve Diversification 

The Committee observed that Ghana's gross international reserves 

increased to approximately US$13.8 billion, providing about 5.7 months 

of import cover by the end of 2025. It was noted that this development 

represents a significant improvement in the country’s external buffer 

position. 

The Comnittee noted that the Bank of Ghana has significantly increased 

its gold reserves under the Domestic Gold Purchase Programme, with 

gold holdings rising from approximately 8.7 tonnes in 2021 to over 40 

tonnes by October 2025, 

1t was posited that this accumulation contributed to strengthening 

Ghana’s international reserves and reducing dependence on foreign 

currency inflows, 

The Committee noted that the Bank’s decision to rebalance the reserve 

portfolio by converting a portion of gold holdings into foreign exchange 

assets in order to maintain an appropriate balance between lquidity, 

safety, and diversification aligns with international reserve management 

practices and enhances the country’s ability to respond to external 

shocks. 

Nevertheless, the Committee emphasised the importance of maintaining 

transparency in reserve management decisions and ensuring that such 

transactions are undertaken based on sound economic ahalysis and risk 

management considerations. 

The Commitiee recommends that the Bank continue to strengthen 

Ghana’s international reserve position by expanding initiatives such as

the domestic gold purchase programme and encouraging policies that 

promote export growth. 

Recovery and Resilience of the Banking Sector 

The Committee observed that Ghana’s banking sector has shown 

significant resilience despite the impact of the domestic debt 

restructuring programme. 

It was noted that the capital adequacy ratio improved to approximately 

17.5 percent, which is above the regulatory minimum of 13 percent. 

The Comrmittee also observed that the non-performing loan ratio declined 

from about 21.8 percent to 18,9 percent, indicating gradual 

improvements in asset quality. 

Additionally, the Committee noted that total assets and deposits in the 

banking industry recorded strong growth during the year, reflecting 

renewed public confidence in tfie financial system. 

The Committee considers the strengthening of the banking sector as 

essential for supporting credit expansion and promoting eccnomic 

recovery and recommends that the Bank maintain robust regulatory 

oversight of the banking sector to ensure that financial institutions 

remain resilient and capable of supporting economic growth 

Access to Credit for Productive Sectors 

The Committee observed that the services sector continues to receive the 

largest share of bank ctedit, while the agricultural sector receives only 

about S percent of total lending. 

The Committee expressed concern that the low level of financing to 

agriculture and manufacturing could undermine efforts to promote job 

creation and industrial growth. 

To address these bottlenecks, it was indicated that the Bank of Ghana 

intenids to promote Jonger-term financing through the capital market and: 

encourage banks to be listed on the stock exchange in order to mobilise 

long-term funds. 

6

6.6.4 

The Cornmittee recommends that the Bank of Ghana should work closely 

with financial institutions to design and implement policies that enhance 

access to affordable credit for productive sectors of the economy, 

particularly agriculture, manufacturing, agro-processing and small and 

medium-sized enterprises. 

In the view of the Committee, allocating a greater proportion of their 

lending portfolios to productive sectors through targeted credit schemes, 

appropriate regulatory incentives and strengthened financial sector 

policies would stimulate domestic production, promote industrial 

growth, and create sustainable employment opportunities. 

Exposure to External and Global Risks 

The Committee observed that while the domestic macroeconomic outlook 

has improved, the Ghanaian economy remains exposed to external 

shocks, particularly fluctuations in commodity prices and geopolitical 

tensions. 

It was revealed that rising global oil prices or prolofiged geopolitical 

conflicts could affect Ghana’s external position and inflation outlook. 

However, the current level of international reserves provides a degree of 

protection against such shocks. 

The Committee therefore emphasised the importance of maintaining 

adequate reserve buffers and continuing prudent macroecononic 

management fo safeguard economic stability. 

The Committee recommends that the Bank should intensify efforts to 

diversify Ghana’s external reserve assets and promote policies that 

increase foreign exchange inflows through exports, remittances, and 

strategic commodity initiatives such as gold and other mineral resources. 

These measures will help cushion the economy against global economic 

uncertainties, commodity price volatility, and fluctuations in 

international financial markets.

7.0 CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATION 

7.1 The Committee has examined the Report on the Conduct of Monetary 

Policy, Macroeconomic Review and Banking Sector Development for the 

period January to December 2025 and has observed that the Bank of 

Ghana generally performed well in relation to the significant 

improvements in key macroeconomic indicators, particularly the decline 

in inflation, the stabilisation and appreciation of the Ghanaian Cedi, the 

improvement in Ghana’s gross international reserves and the resilience 

of the banking sector. The Committee acknowledges that these positive 

developments are largely attributable to the prudent monetary policy 

measures implemented by the Bank of Ghana in collaboration with other 

economic institutions. 

7.2 The Committee, however, observes that despite the progress made, the 

economy remains vulnerable to both domestic and external shocks, 

Issues relating to high lending rates, access to credit for productive 

sectors and exposure to global economic uncertainties continue to 

require sustained policy attention. 

7.3 The Cominittee commends the Bank of Ghana for fulfilling its obligations 

- under Section’53A of the Bank of Ghana (Amendment) Act 2016, (Act 

918) and accordingly urges the House to adopt its Report. 

Respectfully submitted.

text:
REPUBLIC OF GHANA

OF THE

COMMITTEE OF INQUIRY

(Ghana National Procurement Agency)

AWARD OF CONTRACT

FOR

IMPORTATION OF CLINKER

1978

*

REPORT OF THE COIVIMITTEE OF INQUIRY (GHANA
NATIONAL PROCUREMENT AGENCY)—AWARD OF
CONTRACT FOR IMPORTATION OF CLINICER

A.l. We the undersigned Members of the Committee of Inquiry
were appointed on 21st August, 1978 under Executive Instrument No. 149
with the following terms of reference:—

(r/) to mvestigate the circun^tances Icadmg to the award of
$6.6 million contract to Great Company Limited of Switzer
land in this instrument refeired to as the Contractors for
the importation of clinker;

(b) to inquire into the competitive nature of the price quoted
for the award of the contract;

(c) to examine anq determine (he quality of clinker delivered in
Ghana by the Contractors;

(cl) to determine the extent to which the programme for the
shipment of the clinker has been departed from;

(e) to determine the quantities of clinker actually delivered and
the transfers of foreign exchange made by the Bank of
Ghana in payment of such deliveries; and

(f) to submit its findings and recommendations to the Supreme
Military Council not later than the 7th day of September,
1978 giving reasons for their findings and making such
recommendations as the Committee may think fit.

A.2. Procedure

The Committee immediately set out to discharge its duties by collect
ing from the National Procurement Agency all the available and relevant
data concerning the contract foi the importation of the 200,000 metric
tonnes of clinker for the use of Ghana Cement Works Limited. For
convenience and the limited time at our disposal, we held 15 sitting in
camera in all hearing evidence from the Management of_ the Ghana
National Procurement Agency, Ghana Cement Works Limited, Ghana
National Trading Corporation, officials of Ghana Commercial Bank and
Bank of Ghana, the three Commissioners for Trade, Industries and
Special Duties at the Castle as well as other witnesses suniraoned betore
us from time to time including representatives of the clinker manumc-
turers from Poland. For the list of witnesses {vide Appendix ‘ A ). The
Committee also visited the Teraa Plant of the Ghana Cement Works
Limited to examine at the port the storage and discharging facilities for
clinker and also vvent on board a Norwegian vessel which was dis-
charguig clinker from Norway.

A.3. Background to the Setting up of the Committee

For about ten years, i.e. from 1968 to the end of 1977, NORCEM

F.l. The Quantities of Clinker Delivered

Evidence before the Committee revealed that tlie present system of'
using the draught of the vessel in calculating the tonnage of clinker
delivered to Ghana at any particular time is most unsatisfactory. This
method suffers from human errors in visual observation of ship’s draught
readings and manual calculation. Furthermore, a vessel continues to
burn fuel, use water and other provisions even while off-loading clinker.

Besides, the following ship and sea conditions affect draught mark
reading:

(a) Salinity and density of the sea,

(b) Temperature of the sea,

(c) Trim, list, hog and sag of the vessel,
(d) “ Sea State ”.

A clinker vessel, like all other vessels, sometimes drops her anchors i'
bad weather when berthing alongside. The pull of the anchor can affect
the draugltt reading of the ship. All these are factors which could cause

a discrepancy between the tonnage of clinker paid for and the actual
tonnage delivered. However based on this method of calculation the

actual clinker delivered as at 21st August was 87,047 metric tonnes.

G.l. Circumstances Leading to the Award of the Contract

There was evidence before the Committee that the former Chief Exe
cutive of the G.N.P.A., Mr. K. A. Karikciri in entering into the contract
with Great Cape of Lausanne in Switzerland, disregarded all the laid-
down proceduresfor the award and execution of such contract by the Agency
in that:

(/) he not directed by the Board of Directors as he stated
in the agreement signed by him, for and on behafof G.N.P.A.
and the Ghana National Trading Corporation as agents for
Great Cape;

{ii) the contract did not conform to legal standards especially
considering the amount of money involved; i.e. the contract
was sketchy, unprofessional and incomplete.

(Hi) Mr. Karikari deliberately concealed the details of the contract
from all Board Members, who as a rule, should have seen
such details. His reason for concealing the details from the
Board members was that he was afraid that leakage of vital-
information concernng the contract might frustrate his
efforts and that of the Government in breaking the monopoly
which existing suppliers had been enjoying. This the Com
mittee found unconvincing since it impugns the integrity of
Commissioners of State. For, whereas he could not trust
Commissioners of State, he quite willingly divulged the said
vital information to certain officials of the G.N.T.C.

(iv) The former Chief Executive did ot circulate copies of the
contract in accordance with laid-down procedure and up
to the time of sitting. Members, of the Board had not seen

APPENDIX “ H

TEST REPORT ON PENAVEL, BAGRU AND BIAKH
OF 24/5, 26/5 AND 31/5/78

Parallel tests were carried out on clinker received on Peiiavel (Vicat),
Bagru ahd Biakh as to the quality of each clinker.

There was an original sample brought by Penapel and in addition
to this sample Mini samples were collected from the conveyor belts
during discharge at intervals of one hour. These were mixed to form one
major sample.

Similar samples were collected from Bagru and Biakh.

Quality tests were performed as follows:—

I. The SO3 content of the Penavel clinker was very low 0,5 per
cent as compared with approx 2 per cent of both Bagru and
Biakh. Tn order not to waste gypsum it was recommended
that the clinker be ground with SO3 per cent approx. 1.8
per cent. This percentage wUl not impair the quality of the
cement produced.

2. Sieve analysis was carried out and the results conformed
with the normal size from Norway clinker. The outward
examination suggested overburnt clinker.

3. GrindubiUty.—Comparative grinding test with blaine against
time was performd. The Penavel clinker attained the highest
blaine within the shortest possible time even though the
others were very smooth. During grinding very low pro
duction was recorded with Penavel. Due to particles passing
through to cliz and blocking diaphragms.

4. Compressive strength.—The original sample from the ship
was not sufficient for both concrete and mortar tests. How
ever the sample collected during discharging gave lowest
results as compred with Bagru an Biakh samples. However
the quality fulfilled the requirements of Ghana Standards.

5. Chemical Analyses.—Vicat or Penavel clinker showed
highest CaO content. Still the results conformed to Ghana
Standards.

Conclusion.—To achieve maximum production Penavel
clinker has to be mixed with the others during grinding.
From the retention percentage on 4,900 and 10,000 mesh,
it will be very difficult to grind that alone.
